answer.summary:
The field rests on two Stanford/MIT/Toyota Research Institute papers. Severson et al. (2019) showed that simple features of the discharge-voltage curve from the first 100 cycles predict cycle life before capacity fades. Attia et al. (2020) used that early predictor inside a Bayesian-optimization loop, cutting the search over 224 fast-charging protocols from more than 500 days to 16. Later work moved in three directions.

1. Better degradation features. These include resistance at low state of charge right after formation (Weng), Q(V) features from formation (Rhyu, Joule 2025), internal resistance (DCIR) and impedance features that carry across manufacturers (Sours 2024), and work on knee onset and its mechanisms (Attia's knee review, curvature- and physics-based knee prediction).
2. Generalization across operating conditions and chemistries. This line runs from hierarchical Bayesian models on deliberately varied usage conditions (Li et al., 225 NMC cells) to inter-cell deep learning (Nature Machine Intelligence 2025), large benchmarks (BatteryML, BatteryLife) and pretrained models across datasets (PBT). The consistent finding is that models fitted to one narrow lab dataset, often the LFP fast-charge dataset, degrade badly out of distribution. Features linked to mechanisms, such as resistance and degradation modes, transfer better than raw curve statistics.
3. Closed-loop design. This has grown from Bayesian optimization over parameterized constant-current steps to Bayesian-optimized model-predictive control and, most recently, LLM-driven searches over freer protocol forms. Most of these are simulation-heavy compared with Attia's experimental loop.

Physics-informed and hybrid models (Schaeffer tutorial, transferable knee framework) are the main proposed answer to generalization limits. Field-to-lab transfer and dynamic, real-world protocols (chemistry-aware randomized testing) are where the newest work is heading.
gaps: Search date 2026-10-08. Semantic Scholar and OpenAlex were throttled or timed out on most calls, and both citation-graph expansions failed. The list therefore leans on arXiv and web search and is likely missing well-cited journal papers that never appeared on arXiv.

Citation links come from known dataset reuse and research lineage, not reference lists read in this session. Only BatteryLife → BatteryML has direct supporting text (its authors describe BatteryML as the previous largest dataset). Treat the other seven as likely but unverified.

Quotes for Severson 2019 and Attia 2020 come from memory and a search snippet; their abstracts were not available through the paper-reading tool. Paulson 2022, Jiang 2021, Rhyu 2025 and the 2024 formation/electrode-utilization paper have no verified quote. The DOI for Jiang 2021 was not confirmed, so its URL points to a group PDF.

Not covered for lack of budget: Fermín-Cueto et al. on early knee/knee-onset prediction (not found), Aykol et al.'s perspective on combining physics and ML for lifetime prediction (JES 2021), the Stanford/Toyota Research Institute follow-ups on dataset bias and on predicting real-world (non-lab) lifetime, and Nature Energy or Joule papers from 2025-26 on lifetime under dynamic use.

Research gaps in the field: (1) Closed-loop fast-charging optimization has been shown experimentally mainly on commercial LFP cells at 25-30 °C, and transfer to other chemistries, temperatures and pack-level constraints is largely untested. (2) Early predictors are mostly trained on constant-protocol lab cycling and ignore calendar aging and rest periods. (3) Knees are often driven by mechanisms such as lithium plating and electrolyte depletion whose early signals may be electrochemically undetectable, which caps how well early prediction can work. (4) There is no standard out-of-distribution benchmark split; BatteryLife drops formation cycles, and cross-chemistry formation datasets are scarce. (5) Field data and lab data remain poorly connected.

answer.summary: The field starts from two papers by the same group. Severson et al. (2019) predicted cycle life from discharge-voltage-curve (ΔQ(V)) features before any capacity fade appeared, on 124 LFP cells under fast-charging conditions. Attia et al. (2020) then used that early predictor inside a closed Bayesian-optimization loop, which cut the search for good fast-charging protocols from more than 500 days to 16. Follow-ups split three ways. (1) Feature engineering and interpretability: Attia's capacity matrix, Greenbank & Howey's piecewise-linear models, quantile forests for uncertainty, and degradation-mode or incremental-capacity features (Li et al. 2024; Cheng et al. 2024). (2) Generalization: Sulzer et al. found ΔQ(V) variance still correlates with end of life across C-rates and temperatures. Hierarchical Bayesian models separate cycling-condition effects from manufacturing variation. BatLiNet's inter-cell learning (401 cells, 168 conditions), DCIR features that transfer across manufacturers, and the PBT foundation model work to transfer across chemistries and designs. Discovery Learning (Nature 2025) goes further and predicts the life of new pouch-cell designs zero-shot. (3) Closed-loop and control: newer work moves from Bayesian optimization over fixed six-step protocols to safe Bayesian optimization tuning MPC chargers, and to LLM-driven protocol search over much larger protocol spaces. Two results expose the limits of generalization. The knee review shows some aging pathways are electrochemically invisible early on, which caps what early data can predict. Geslin et al. (2025) find that realistic dynamic discharge profiles extend life by up to 38% compared with constant-current lab cycling, so models trained on lab protocols may be biased in real use. Feature-based linear and Bayesian models still lead on small datasets and interpretability. Deep and inter-cell models do better once data are pooled across conditions.

Field-data validation remains thin. Nearly all models are trained on lab cycling under fixed protocols. Dynamic and real-world loads, calendar aging and temperature extremes are underrepresented.

Closed-loop charging optimization is still mostly limited to a single cell chemistry and format (LFP 18650 in Attia 2020). Transfer of optimized protocols across chemistries, temperatures and cell formats is largely untested.

Predicting knees early, and quantifying uncertainty when conditions fall outside the training data, are still open problems. Safety-relevant effects such as lithium plating under fast charging are rarely predicted directly.

answer.summary:
The field starts with two papers. Severson et al. (2019) showed that features from early-cycle discharge voltage curves (ΔQ(V)) predict cycle life before capacity fade is visible. Attia et al. (2020) used that predictor inside a closed loop with Bayesian optimization to rank fast-charging protocols in days instead of months.

Follow-up work went three ways:
- **Better degradation features:** interpretable statistical learning (Attia 2021), systematic feature engineering (Paulson 2022), impedance spectra (Zhang 2020), knee-point detection (Fermín-Cueto 2020; the Attia 2022 knees review) and formation-stage diagnostics (Weng 2021).
- **Fast-charging optimization:** constrained Bayesian optimization in simulation (Jiang/Braatz 2022), feature-driven closed loops (2023), and in 2024 reinforcement learning with safety constraints and Bayesian optimization tuning of MPC controllers.
- **Generalization:** the main concern of 2024–2026 work. BatLiNet's inter-cell learning (2025), hierarchical Bayesian models under varied usage (Li 2024), physics-informed networks (Wang 2024), the BatteryLife benchmark (2025, about 998 cells), and Discovery Learning (Nature, 2025/26) all try to transfer across protocols, temperatures, chemistries and cell designs.

At the same time, Geslin et al. (2025) found that realistic dynamic discharge profiles give up to 38% more lifetime than constant-current tests. That questions whether lab-trained predictors and lab-optimized charging protocols hold up in real use, the same point Sulzer (2021) and Aitio and Howey (2021) made about field data.

Overall, single-dataset early prediction works well. Accuracy still drops out of distribution, especially for knees, new chemistries and dynamic or field use.

Caveats: the research-call budget ran out before I could open the Nature pages, which redirected to a login. Quotes for Severson and Attia 2020 come from memory of the abstracts, and many quote fields are empty rather than invented. The citation links come only from BatteryLife's reference list, a search result saying Discovery Learning cites BatLiNet, and the fact that Attia 2020 directly builds on Severson 2019. Some DOIs (Paulson, Attia 2021, the knees review, Weng, Aitio) are from memory and were not checked in this session.
gaps: Lab-to-field transfer: most models are trained on constant-current lab cycling, and Geslin 2025 shows dynamic profiles change lifetime substantially. There are few field-validated lifetime predictors.

Closed-loop fast-charging optimization has mostly been shown on a single LFP/graphite cell type with fixed-time multistep protocols. Optimal protocols carrying over to other chemistries, formats, temperatures or degraded cells is largely untested.
Early predictors often miss knee or rapid-fade onset that has not yet shown up in early-cycle features. Knee-aware predictions with uncertainty remain immature.
Benchmarks such as BatteryLife and BatteryML show large performance drops across domains. There is no standard out-of-distribution protocol (held-out chemistry, temperature or protocol splits).
Calendar aging and rest periods, which mix with cycling, are rarely modelled together in early-prediction or charging-optimization work.
Closed loops usually optimize lifetime alone. Multi-objective optimization (lifetime, charge time, plating safety, heat) with physics-based constraints in real experiments is sparse.
Commercial large-format and next-generation chemistries (Si-rich anodes, sodium-ion, solid-state) are underrepresented in public data, which limits claims of general models.
This review is incomplete: the research-call budget ended before I could check full texts, reference lists or abstracts for several 2024–2026 preprints.

answer.summary:
Note on reliability: I used all 8 research calls, and only some of this list was checked against a live page. The BatLiNet, Discovery Learning and lab–field bridging entries were confirmed on their arXiv pages. BatteryLife, the impedance-across-manufacturers preprint and Attia 2020 were confirmed through search results. Several DOIs and exact titles are from memory and should be checked before citing: Paulson 2022, Weng 2021, Sulzer 2021, Aitio & Howey 2021, Geslin 'Dynamic cycling' and Jiang 2022. Only a few quotes were actually seen: three in search snippets (Attia 2020, BatteryLife, the impedance preprint) and one on an arXiv page (BatLiNet). The Severson quote is recalled from memory and was not checked. Every other quote is left blank. The citation links rest on strong evidence (shared datasets or groups, or statements in search results). They are not checked against full reference lists.

How the field developed: Severson et al. (2019) showed that hand-crafted features of the early-cycle discharge curve, chiefly the variance of ΔQ(V), predict cycle life before capacity fade is visible. Attia et al. (2020) turned that predictor into a cheap proxy reward inside Bayesian optimization, cutting charging-protocol search from more than 500 days to 16. Follow-ups split into three lines:
1. **Better degradation features:** knee and knee-onset definitions, impedance spectra, formation-stage features and systematic feature studies.
2. **Better closed-loop design:** constrained Bayesian optimization, Bayesian-optimization-tuned model-predictive control, and RL-based charging.
3. **Generalization:** much of the recent work (2024–26) tackles the narrowness of single-chemistry, constant-current lab datasets, using inter-cell deep learning (BatLiNet), large multi-source benchmarks (BatteryLife, BatteryML), impedance features that transfer across manufacturers, zero-shot or active 'Discovery Learning' for industrial cells, chemistry-aware models and lab-to-field bridging.

There is a trade-off. Feature-based linear or GP models are interpretable and data-efficient but transfer poorly. Deep, pooled-data models transfer better but are less interpretable and depend on how heterogeneous the datasets are. Geslin et al. (dynamic cycling) show that the lab protocols themselves can bias lifetime labels.
gaps: Closed-loop charging optimization is still mostly single-chemistry (LFP/graphite 18650) and single-objective. I found no confirmed peer-reviewed 2025–26 successor to Attia 2020 that optimizes charging across chemistries or formats.
Early predictors are trained under constant-current or fixed-protocol cycling. Dynamic-cycling results suggest the lifetime labels themselves change under realistic use, which is largely unaddressed.
Evidence from field data is scarce. Most transfer studies still use public lab datasets, and lab-to-field bridging is shown on only a few cell types.
Interaction of the proxy model with the optimizer: errors or bias in the early-life predictor can mislead Bayesian-optimization protocol selection, and this is rarely quantified.
Calendar aging, rest periods and path dependence (varying conditions over a cell's life) are underrepresented in cycle-life prediction benchmarks.
Uncertainty calibration under distribution shift (new chemistry, temperature or manufacturer) is seldom reported. Most papers report point-estimate MAPE or RMSE.
Knee prediction remains fragile because knee definitions are inconsistent and the mechanisms (plating, electrolyte depletion, loss of active material) are rarely tied to the ML features.
Several 2025–26 items here (Discovery Learning, the GPT-based Nature Communications paper, chemistry-aware prediction) could not be fully checked within the tool budget.

answer.summary:
Three sorbent strategies dominate DAC research.

(1) Amine-appended MOFs (mmen-Mg2(dobpdc) in 2012, the cooperative-insertion mechanism in 2015, tetraamine variants in 2020) bind CO2 chemically. This gives large uptake at 0.4 mbar, and the same material also works at the 0.15 bar of flue gas. Water is generally tolerated or even helpful: humid air switches the cooperative step-shaped uptake into a simple type I isotherm, and steam can be used for regeneration. The open questions are oxidative and thermal amine loss and slow kinetics in very dilute feeds.

(2) Ultramicroporous physisorbents (SIFSIX-3-Ni/Cu, CALF-20) rely on strong pore confinement instead of chemistry. They do well on CO2-rich or dry streams, and CALF-20 holds up at 40% RH under flue-gas conditions. However, the Kumar 2015 benchmark shows that atmospheric moisture sharply cuts their DAC performance. This is the clearest split between flue-gas and air conditions: at 400 ppm CO2 the water/CO2 ratio is about 25–50×, so H2O competition matters far more than in flue gas.

(3) Newer frameworks, mainly amine-grafted COFs (COF-999 in 2024, ImCOF-TAEA in 2026) plus charged sorbents, have strong covalent backbones, uptake that increases with humidity, and regeneration at about 60 °C. COF-999 has been cycled outdoors.

On the computational side, OpenDAC 2023 and 2025 provide tens of millions of DFT calculations of CO2/H2O (and N2/O2) adsorption in MOFs, plus ML potentials. They are complemented by intrinsic energy and purity limits, checks of flexible force fields, and a 2026 argument that dry screening criteria break down in humid air.

Process-level studies have moved from monolith TVSA cost models (Sinha et al.: $60–190/t for mmen-Mg2(dobpdc)) through parametric and sorbent-focused TEAs and an LCA of an industrial plant to bed-geometry optimisation ($49–116/t). Across these, sorbent lifetime, cycle time and water co-adsorption (Young et al. 2021) come out as the main cost drivers, more than equilibrium capacity alone.

answer.summary:
Four strands run through this list.

1. **Amine-appended MOFs (diamine–Mg2(dobpdc)).** This line runs from McDonald 2012 and 2015 through step tuning in 2017 and higher-capacity variants in 2024. These are the only MOFs with strong documented uptake at 0.4 mbar CO2. The same platform can be shifted to flue gas by changing the diamine (dmpn, 2-ampd). In flue gas, water can even help (2-ampd, 2019). Humid-air work from 2024–25 (lattice theory, co-adsorption modelling, amine-impregnated tests) shows a different picture: water breaks the cooperative chain mechanism and turns step isotherms into Langmuir-type ones. That makes humid-air behaviour hard to predict from dry or flue-gas data.

2. **Ultramicroporous physisorbents (SIFSIX-3-Cu/Ni, other hybrid ultramicroporous materials, CALF-20).** Tight pores give excellent selectivity at trace CO2 levels with low regeneration energy. However, Kumar 2015 and Madden 2016 showed that moisture cuts DAC performance badly. CALF-20's water tolerance has been shown for flue gas (about 40% RH, 15% CO2), not for 400 ppm air.

3. **Newer frameworks.** The polyamine-grafted COF-999 (2024) is a polyamine-grafted COF that takes up more CO2 at 50% RH than dry and has been tested in outdoor air. Here the chemistry, not the framework class, decides humidity tolerance.

4. **Screening and process studies.** ODAC23 and ODAC25 provide DFT and ML-potential data with explicit H2O co-adsorption. Intrinsic-DAC metrics bound energy use and purity from material properties alone. Process studies (Sabatino 2021, Wiegner 2022, Balasubramaniam 2024) show that ambient humidity and temperature, and cycle design, drive energy use and cost as much as isotherms do.

**Air vs flue gas:** Flue gas (about 4–15% CO2, hot, humid) favours physisorbents and diamine–MOFs with moderate binding. Air (about 400 ppm, variable RH) needs chemisorption or very tight pores, and water competition or mechanism changes become the deciding factor.

**Citation links:** Only two are recorded: ODAC25 → ODAC23, and Madden 2016 → Kumar 2015 (that abstract refers back to the earlier study).
gaps: The citation-graph expansion failed: Semantic Scholar was rate-limiting and OpenAlex was over its daily budget. Two of the four searches also timed out, so forward-citation coverage of 2024–2026 work is incomplete and most likely citation links between listed papers are unconfirmed (e.g., later work citing McDonald 2012 or Kumar 2015).

No abstract was retrieved for COF-999 (Nature 2024), McDonald 2015 (Nature), Sabatino 2021 (Joule) or Balasubramaniam 2024 (CEJ), so their quotes are empty. COF-999 figures come from secondary web sources.
The quote for the 2025 amine-impregnated Mg2(dobpdc) paper comes from a search summary, not a direct read of the abstract.

Not verified, so not listed: Gu & Li 2026 (Carbon Capture Sci. Technol.) on humid-air screening criteria, the TAEA@MIL-101(Cr) DAC benchmark (ACS Cent. Sci. 2026), and the 2025 surrogate-assisted TVSA optimisation of mmen-Mg2(dobpdc) (Sep. Purif. Technol.).

Under-covered: supported-amine and aminopolymer silica (Climeworks-type) sorbents, alkali carbonates, zeolites for DAC, moisture-swing ion-exchange resins, and recent MOFs designed for DAC (e.g., MUF-16, Al-formate, amine-grafted MOF-808 and other Zr MOFs).
No dedicated humid-air vs flue-gas head-to-head benchmark appeared. Most physisorbent humidity data are from flue-gas or near-flue-gas conditions.

Search date: 2026-10-08. The arXiv preprints listed (ODAC25, Intrinsic DAC, ML force-field comparison) are listed under their arXiv versions; I did not check whether they have since been published in journals.

answer.summary:
I found 24 papers. The research budget (8 searches) only let me confirm a few details: most DOIs and titles are from memory, and the only quotes kept come from abstract text that searches returned. I'd check DOIs before citing them. Of the 6 citation links, only 3 are documented. ODAC25 extends ODAC23, a 2025 correspondence critiques ODAC23, and the 2019 SIFSIX-18 paper builds on the group's 2015 physisorbent benchmark. The other 3 are links within the same research groups that I expected but did not check.

Main finding: whether water is present matters more than whether the CO2 source is air or flue gas.

- **Amine-appended frameworks (chemisorbents):** These include mmen-CuBTTri, diamine-Mg2(dobpdc) and COF-999. They bind CO2 as carbamate chains (cooperative insertion), so they hold strongly enough to capture at 400 ppm, and water is usually neutral or helpful. COF-999 doubles its uptake at 50% humidity, and mmen-Mg2(dobpdc) is stable up to 50% humidity. The weak points are amine loss and degradation, the regeneration temperature, and changes in uptake behaviour when the air is humid.
- **Ultramicroporous physisorbents (SIFSIX/TIFSIX, CALF-20):** These excel when the gas is dry or concentrated. CALF-20 works on humid flue gas because CO2 at about 10–15% can outcompete water. At 400 ppm with typical humidity, though, water usually displaces CO2. The proposed fixes are hydrophobic pore design (SIFSIX-18-Ni-β), short cycles that exploit slow water uptake (TIFSIX-3-Ni), or drying the air first.
- **Computational screening:** The Open DAC datasets (ODAC23, then ODAC25) scaled DFT and machine-learning screening to about 15,000 MOFs with H2O, N2 and O2 included. A 2025 critique and a 2026 process-aware screen argue that single-site binding descriptors and Henry-regime thresholds mislead under humid air. They recommend ranking by process-level working capacity and regeneration energy that includes the cost of desorbing co-adsorbed water.
- **Process studies:** Sabatino et al. (Joule 2021) and steam-assisted temperature–vacuum swing cycle models find that capital cost and productivity, not sorbent binding energy, dominate DAC cost. The integrated materials-to-process platform in Nature 2024 is aimed mainly at flue-gas capture.
gaps: Only 8 searches were allowed, so most DOIs were not confirmed. Quotes are given only where abstract text came back from a search.

Several citation links are expected same-group lineage (McDonald 2015 → 2012, Kim 2020 → McDonald 2015, Shekhah 2014 → Nugent 2013) rather than checked against reference lists. COF-999's references to the amine-MOF papers and the 2026 screen's references to ODAC were not checked either.
Few 2025–2026 experimental papers on amine-MOF or ultramicroporous sorbents tested under realistic humid DAC conditions turned up. Any recent Nature or Science MOF-for-DAC papers may be missing.

Long-term durability under real outdoor air (O2, SOx/NOx, temperature swings) beyond about 100 cycles is barely covered for MOFs and COFs. Scalable synthesis and shaping into contactors (monoliths, fibers) are not covered.

Process studies that use measured MOF or COF isotherms (rather than generic amine-on-support sorbents) for full DAC plant cost estimates are scarce. Promising 2024 TVSA papers were left out because their exact titles could not be confirmed: a capacity-fade cost model (Energy Environ. Sci. 2024, d4ee00616j) and an air pre-drying (dehumidification) cost study.
Sub-ambient and cold-climate DAC, and comparisons with zeolites, polymeric amines and alkali-carbonate sorbents, were left out.

answer.summary:
I found 25 papers in four groups, listed roughly from foundational to recent.

**Air vs flue gas, by material family**
- **Amine-appended MOFs.** mmen- and diamine-Mg2(dobpdc) capture CO2 cooperatively, by inserting it into metal–amine bonds. That gives sharp step isotherms and large working capacities at flue-gas pressures (5–15% CO2). At 400 ppm, many variants have their step at or above the air CO2 pressure. In humid air, water changes how the CO2 binds (the 2024 ExxonMobil cooperative-lattice study).
- **Ultramicroporous physisorbents** (SIFSIX, NbOFFIVE, TIFSIX; CALF-20 for flue gas). Pore size and fluorinated pillars give strong CO2 physisorption at trace concentrations with mild regeneration. Their weakness is that water competes for sites at ambient humidity. NbOFFIVE-1-Ni and SIFSIX-18-Ni-β are the main humidity-tolerant exceptions.
- **Newer frameworks.** Grafted or grown amines in water-stable frameworks (COF-999, amine-functionalized MOF-808, NUS-110) reverse the humidity penalty. Bicarbonate forms in humid air, so capacity and kinetics improve with water, and regeneration runs at about 60 °C. This is the clearest DAC-specific design trend of 2024–2025. Most claims rest on lab or small outdoor tests, and some performance comparisons (e.g., COF-999 versus MOFs) come from the material's developers.

**Computational screening**
The work moved from wet-flue-gas screening (Boyd 2019) to DFT/ML datasets built for DAC (ODAC23, then ODAC25 with H2O/N2/O2 included). A 2026 study argues that single-point descriptors such as Henry's constants and heats of adsorption mis-rank sorbents unless the screening models a full humid-air cycle.

**Process-level analyses**
Studies range from the first MOF TVSA design (Sinha 2017, roughly $75–200/t, with water co-adsorption not modeled in detail) to the Joule comparison (Sabatino 2021) and 2024 studies. The 2024 work shows that dry CO2 capacity matters less than water handling, steam use and dehumidification. One 2024 study puts the best case at about $194/t with pre-drying to 40% RH.

**Conclusion**
The best flue-gas sorbents (high CO2 partial pressure, hot wet gas, steam regeneration) are rarely the best for DAC (400 ppm CO2, about 20–80% RH, low-grade heat). Reliable ranking needs measurements and models under humid, cyclic conditions.

**Caveats on this list**
- Citation links include only pairs with direct evidence or obvious lineage (e.g., ODAC25 extends ODAC23).
- Several quotes are empty because I couldn't verify the abstract text within the search budget.
- Some DOIs were recalled from memory and not checked online, including Sinha 2017 IECR and Bhatt 2016 JACS.
gaps: No independent long-term outdoor field data (thousands of cycles, real temperature and humidity swings, SOx/NOx/O3 exposure) for any MOF or COF DAC sorbent. COF-999 reports about 100 cycles.
Results from different humidity protocols are hard to compare (30% vs 50% RH, equilibrium vs breakthrough, flue-gas temperatures vs ambient), and there is no standard humid-DAC test.
Oxidative degradation of amine-appended frameworks in air, and the steam stability of ultramicroporous fluorinated MOFs, are reported far less than capacity.

Computational datasets (ODAC23/25) cover mostly rigid, non-amine MOFs. They do not represent chemisorption on grafted amines or cooperative insertion well, and they lack cycle-level humid-air metrics.
Few process or cost studies use measured humid co-adsorption isotherms for newer sorbents (COF-999, MOF-808-amines, NUS-110). Most still model mmen-Mg2(dobpdc), MIL-101-PEI or generic amine sorbents.
Life-cycle and cost analyses of making MOFs and COFs at large scale (linker cost, solvents) for megatonne DAC are sparse. TIFSIX-3-Ni and CALF-20 are partial exceptions.
I could not verify abstract quotes or full bibliographic details for several papers within the 8-call budget.

answer.summary:
I could not verify the citation links against an index: the citation-graph lookups failed, so every link is inferred (details in the gaps).

**Before DPO.** The RLHF line runs from Christiano et al. (2017), which learned reward models from pairwise human preferences, through Ziegler (2019), Stiennon (2020), InstructGPT (2022) and Anthropic HH (2022). Those papers set the standard pipeline: fit a reward model, then optimize a KL-regularized objective with PPO, an online method that needs several models at once.

**DPO itself.** DPO shows that this KL-regularized objective has a closed-form optimal policy. That makes the log-ratio between the policy and a reference model an implicit reward, so one offline classification loss replaces both the reward model and PPO. SLiC-HF and RRHF were contrastive or ranking losses from the same period, and RSO later placed SLiC and DPO in a common framework.

**Follow-ups, in three directions.**
- **Generalizing the loss:** IPO/ΨPO removes the assumption that pairwise preferences can be turned into pointwise rewards. NCA/InfoNCA covers scalar rewards and contains DPO as a special case. DiscoPOP searches for new loss functions automatically. "From r to Q*" re-derives DPO at the token level.
- **Removing the reference model:** CPO, ORPO (an odds-ratio term added to SFT) and SimPO (length-normalized reward plus a margin) save memory and compute. The cost is losing the explicit KL anchor to the reference model.
- **Learning from unpaired feedback:** KTO uses a prospect-theory utility on binary desirable/undesirable labels, so it needs no preference pairs.

**Critiques.** Xu et al. (2024) and Tajwar et al. (2024) argue that purely offline DPO-style training lags well-tuned PPO or on-policy data.

**Open recipes at scale.** Recipes evolved from Zephyr (DPO on AI feedback) to Tülu 2+DPO at 70B, then Tülu 3 (SFT → DPO → RLVR) and OLMo 2. Modern open recipes keep DPO as the preference stage and add online RL with verifiable rewards. Work in 2026, such as Normalized Rewards, is still reshaping the implicit reward.
gaps: The citation-graph lookups failed in this session (Semantic Scholar timeouts and throttling, OpenAlex HTTP 429), so research_expand returned nothing. No link was checked against a citation index. Links come from method names in the abstracts I read, plus my own knowledge of these papers' reference lists. Treat the links from DPO to its foundations, from SimPO to its baselines (ORPO, KTO, IPO, CPO) and from Tülu 3 to Tülu 2 and SimPO as likely but unconfirmed.

Search date was 2026-10-08. Only arXiv returned search results, so recent 2025–2026 work is under-sampled. Candidates not screened in depth: ξ-DPO (arXiv 2605.10981), Mitigating Mismatch within Reference-based Preference Optimization (2602.11902), SLIME (2602.02383), Boosting DPO with Penalization (2606.12505).

Not covered for lack of tool budget: online and iterative DPO (self-rewarding LMs, OAIF, iterative DPO), Nash/game-theoretic methods (Nash-MD, SPPO, DNO), length-controlled and regularized DPO (R-DPO), and β-DPO / TDPO.

Large-model reports that use DPO at scale (Llama 3, Qwen2/2.5, DeepSeek-V3) and GRPO-based recipes (DeepSeekMath, DeepSeek-R1) were left out because their abstracts do not establish the DPO link. Llama 3's post-training reportedly uses DPO.

answer.summary:
How the field developed: RLHF started with reward learning from pairwise comparisons (Christiano 2017), then KL-regularized fine-tuning of language models with PPO (Ziegler 2019, Stiennon 2020), and scaled up in InstructGPT and Anthropic's HH work. DPO (2023) showed that the optimal policy of this KL-regularized objective has a closed form under Bradley-Terry preferences. That means the reward model and the PPO stage can be replaced by a single logistic loss on (chosen, rejected) pairs, with the reference policy acting as an implicit regularizer.

The follow-ups split into three groups:
1. **Generalizing the loss.** IPO/ΨPO drops the Bradley-Terry-to-pointwise-reward assumption and resists overfitting. GPO treats DPO, IPO and SLiC as choices of a convex loss. f-DPO and f-PO replace the reverse KL with general f-divergences. RSO and SLiC are close relatives, built on sampling and calibration respectively.
2. **Removing the reference model.** CPO, ORPO and SimPO drop the reference policy. They use a likelihood regularizer, an odds ratio folded into SFT, and a length-normalized log-probability with a margin, respectively. SimPER goes further and removes the tunable hyperparameters.
3. **Learning from unpaired feedback.** KTO uses a prospect-theory utility on per-example good/bad labels, so it needs no pairs.

Analysis papers (r→Q*, Is DPO superior to PPO?, overoptimization scaling laws) show that direct alignment algorithms still overoptimize, and that well-tuned online PPO can beat them.

At scale, Zephyr made DPO on AI-labelled UltraFeedback data a standard approach. Llama 3 used DPO instead of PPO. Tülu 3 published a fully open SFT → DPO → RLVR recipe that compared DPO with SimPO-style variants and kept length-normalized DPO. OLMo 2 reused that recipe. The overall trend: offline preference optimization has become a cheap middle stage, increasingly followed by online RL with verifiable rewards.

answer.summary:
**Where DPO comes from.** The upstream pipeline is: Christiano et al. (2017) learn a reward from pairwise preferences (Bradley-Terry); Ziegler et al. (2019) and Stiennon et al. (2020) apply this to language models with KL-penalized PPO; InstructGPT and Anthropic's HH paper scale it into the SFT → reward model → PPO recipe. DPO observes that the optimal policy for the KL-constrained objective has a closed form. Writing the reward in terms of the policy turns RLHF into one logistic loss on preference pairs: no explicit reward model, no sampling, no PPO. SLiC-HF was a concurrent offline hinge-loss alternative.

**Follow-ups split along three axes:**
- **Generalizing the loss.** IPO/ΨPO fixes Bradley-Terry overfitting with a squared loss. GPO puts DPO, IPO and SLiC into one convex-loss family.
- **Removing the reference model.** CPO, ORPO (odds ratio plus SFT, single stage) and SimPO (length-normalized log-probability with a margin) drop the reference policy to save memory and compute. Pre-DPO (2025) argues the reference acts mainly as a data re-weighter.
- **Unpaired feedback.** KTO learns from binary desirable/undesirable labels.

**Open recipes at scale.** Zephyr (DPO on UltraFeedback AI feedback) and Tulu 2 made DPO the default open alignment step. Llama 3 used iterative DPO at 405B instead of PPO. Tulu 3 (Nov 2024) and Olmo 3 (Dec 2025) put DPO on on-policy or "delta" preference pairs between SFT and RL with verifiable rewards (RLVR). So offline preference optimization now serves as a cheap middle stage, not a full replacement for RL.

**Open questions.** Self-Rewarding LMs and "Is DPO Superior to PPO?" show the field moving back toward online/iterative data, on evidence that well-tuned PPO can beat purely offline DPO.

answer.summary:
I found 23 papers. They trace the lineage in four stages.

**1. Reward model + PPO.** Christiano et al. (2017) learned a reward model from pairwise preferences. PPO (2017) became the policy optimizer. Ziegler (2019), Stiennon (2020), InstructGPT (2022) and Anthropic's HH paper (2022) built the standard three-stage pipeline for language models: SFT, then a reward model, then PPO with a KL penalty.

**2. DPO's reformulation.** DPO (2023) showed that the KL-regularized optimum has a closed form. That turns the reward model into an implicit log-ratio against a reference policy, and turns RLHF into a logistic loss over pairs. Similar ranking losses appeared at about the same time in RRHF and SLiC-HF.

**3. Follow-ups, along three axes:**
- **Generalizing the loss:** IPO/ΨPO adds regularization against overfitting on deterministic preferences, and GPO unifies DPO, IPO and SLiC as one convex-loss family.
- **Removing the reference model:** ORPO folds an odds-ratio term into SFT, and SimPO uses a length-normalized reward with a target margin.
- **Learning from unpaired feedback:** KTO uses binary desirable/undesirable labels with a prospect-theory utility.
- **Iterative / online and critiques:** Self-Rewarding LMs run iterative DPO, and "Is DPO Superior to PPO?" argues that well-tuned PPO can still win.

**4. Open recipes at scale.** Zephyr and Tulu 2 made DPO the default for open models. Llama 3 used DPO at frontier scale. Tulu 3 (Nov 2024) settled on SFT → length-normalized DPO → RLVR, and OLMo 2 and Olmo 3 reuse that recipe. In this line, DPO has moved from being the final alignment step to a middle stage before RL with verifiable rewards. Delta Learning (2025) shows that the quality gap within a pair matters more than how good either response is on its own, and Olmo 3 uses that idea.

**Overall:** the trend runs from online RL to offline contrastive losses and back to hybrid pipelines (offline DPO, then online RLVR). Reference-free and unpaired variants trade the KL anchor for simplicity and lower memory cost.

**Evidence for the citation links:** I checked the Tulu 3, OLMo 2, Delta Learning and Olmo 3 abstracts directly. The other links come from well-known reference lists, not from reading each bibliography in this session.
gaps: The search budget was too small to read reference lists, so most citation links come from known bibliographies and weren't checked again here. Lower-confidence links were left out (e.g., KTO→SLiC, ORPO→KTO).

I found no clearly authoritative 2025–2026 paper that is both reference-free and uses unpaired feedback. Newer DPO variants (e.g., temporal-decay DPO, arXiv 2502.14340) weren't verified well enough to include.
The Tulu 2 and Llama 3 entries have no verbatim quotes because I didn't open their abstracts.

Online/on-policy follow-ups (online DPO, RLOO, GRPO in DeepSeek-R1 and Qwen) are only lightly covered. Qwen2.5, DeepSeek-V3, Nemotron and SmolLM3 (which uses APO) are left out even though they use DPO-style objectives.
Other DPO-family variants are missing: CPO, R-DPO/length-regularized DPO, β-DPO, TDPO, Cal-DPO, APO, SPPO, Nash-MD.
Recent mid-2026 work, such as Instella-MoE (arXiv 2609.00791), which reports DPO instability on MoE models, was seen but not verified or included.

answer.summary:
**Starting point.** GRPO (DeepSeekMath, 2024) dropped PPO's critic and replaced it with a group baseline: each response's reward minus the mean reward of its group, divided by the group's standard deviation. It keeps PPO's token-level clipped ratio and adds a KL penalty. DeepSeek-R1 made this the default RLVR recipe. RLOO, a leave-one-out baseline without std normalization, is its closest sibling.

**Objective changes.** Later work splits into three groups.
- **Length bias / loss aggregation:**
  - Dr. GRPO removes the per-response 1/|o| factor and the std normalization.
  - DAPO switches to a token-level loss.
  - λ-GRPO learns the aggregation weights.
  - "Concise Reasoning via RL" argues the length growth comes from losses on incorrect answers.
  - The 2026 impossibility paper shows no weighting scheme can be both unbiased and length-invariant.
- **Reward / advantage normalization:**
  - REINFORCE++ normalizes over the global batch instead of the group.
  - OPO uses a variance-optimal baseline.
  - GPG removes the surrogate loss and KL term.
  - RAFT++/Reinforce-Rej finds that most of GRPO's gain comes from filtering prompts where every response is wrong, not from normalization.
- **Ratio / clipping stability:**
  - DAPO's Clip-Higher.
  - GSPO's sequence-level ratio.
  - GMPO's geometric mean.
  - SAPO's soft gate.
  - CISPO clips the importance-sampling weights.
  - Clip-Cov/KL-Cov target entropy collapse.

**Sampling-level changes.** These sit between objective and system: DAPO's dynamic sampling and GFPO's length-based filtering within larger groups.

**Training-system changes.** Several stability gains come from the training stack, not the loss:
- the FP16 paper fixes BF16 numerical mismatch between rollout engine and trainer;
- AReaL's asynchronous rollouts introduce staleness, which its objective then has to correct for;
- Qwen's formulation paper ties MoE Routing Replay and IS correction to keeping the token-level surrogate valid.

**Caveat on comparing results.** Headline numbers are not directly comparable. Base models differ (Qwen2.5-32B base for DAPO/VAPO, distilled models for Skywork, Phi-4 for GFPO, MoE models for GSPO/SAPO/CISPO), as do datasets, context limits and the AIME metric (avg@k vs pass@1). VAPO-vs-DAPO, "Tricks or Traps" and ScaleRL are the main same-setup comparisons. ScaleRL suggests normalization and aggregation choices mainly change efficiency, not the final ceiling.
gaps: Semantic Scholar and OpenAlex were throttled or timed out (search date 2026-10-08), so the citation graph could not be expanded. Papers were picked from an arXiv-only search plus papers I already knew, then checked by reading their arXiv abstracts.

The citation links listed are not from reference-list data. Each is inferred because the citing paper names the cited method or paper in its abstract (e.g., GRPO→DeepSeekMath, PPO→Schulman et al.). Many more real citations surely exist but are unverified.
The CISPO quote is cut off mid-word because the source abstract was truncated there; the CISPO details in the reason come from my own knowledge, not the abstract.

Some details in the reasons come from my own knowledge rather than the retrieved abstract text. Examples: DAPO's four techniques beyond decoupled clipping and dynamic sampling, AReaL's staleness-correcting objective, and that 'Tricks or Traps' covers normalization, clipping and loss aggregation.

Left out for space but relevant: Kimi k1.5 (2501.12599), Open-Reasoner-Zero (2503.24290), Skywork-OR1 (2505.22312), ProRL (2505.24864), Beyond the 80/20 Rule (2506.01939), Revisiting GRPO on/off-policy (2505.22257), and Mu-GRPO (2605.17570).
Not covered: blog-only work on truncated importance sampling and training–inference mismatch (e.g., the Yao et al. 'off-policy RL framework' post), and the KL-estimator (k3) bias analyses.
Many 2026 arXiv preprints (MHPO, Soft Sequence PO, Range-GRPO, Advantage Clipped PO, etc.) showed up in search but were not screened beyond their titles and snippets.
Process-reward and credit-assignment extensions (GiGPO, BoT-GRPO) and non-text uses of GRPO were excluded as out of scope.

answer.summary:
I found 25 papers; the abstracts of all 25 were checked against arXiv on 2026-10-08.

**Foundations.** GRPO (DeepSeekMath) replaced PPO's critic with a baseline computed within each group of sampled answers: each reward minus the group mean, divided by the group standard deviation. DeepSeek-R1 made this the standard recipe for training reasoning models. RLOO is its main critic-free sibling: it uses a leave-one-out baseline over the other samples.

**Objective changes, by problem.**
- **Length bias:** Dr. GRPO removes the per-response length normalization and the std division. DAPO switches to averaging the loss over tokens and adds overlong reward shaping. A 2026 impossibility theorem shows that no length weighting can be both unbiased and length-invariant, so GRPO and Dr. GRPO sit at opposite ends of one tradeoff.
- **Reward and normalization:**
  - REINFORCE++ and SPO normalize advantages across the whole batch instead of within each group; SPO also drops groups entirely in favour of a persistent value tracker.
  - BNPO uses adaptive Beta-distribution normalization; OPO uses a variance-minimizing optimal baseline.
  - GDPO normalizes each reward separately when there are several.
  - A 2026 curvature analysis argues the std normalization Dr. GRPO dropped actually helps, because it acts as an adaptive gradient.
- **Stability of the update:**
  - GSPO computes importance ratios and clipping per sequence instead of per token. GMPO averages token terms geometrically instead of arithmetically.
  - CISPO clips the importance-sampling weights themselves. DAPO's "clip-higher" loosens the upper clip bound. GVPO builds the KL-constrained optimum into its gradient weights.
  - The entropy-mechanism paper diagnoses entropy collapse.

**Training-system changes (the objective is unchanged).** AReaL runs rollouts asynchronously. The FP16 paper fixes the precision mismatch between rollout and training. Qwen's "Stabilizing RL" paper connects the two views: token-level surrogate objectives are only valid when the train–inference mismatch and policy staleness are small, which explains why importance-sampling correction, clipping and MoE Routing Replay help. DAPO's dynamic sampling is a data/sampling change rather than a loss change.

**Comparing results.** Headline AIME numbers are not comparable across setups. DAPO and VAPO start from the Qwen2.5-32B base model; Skywork-OR1 starts from R1-distilled models; Dr. GRPO uses small models. VAPO's comparison with DAPO is the only "identical settings" claim here, and it is a critic-based method. The controlled ablations (ScaleRL, "Tricks or Traps") find that loss aggregation and normalization mostly change compute efficiency, not final performance. Treat them as the fair comparisons.
gaps: Semantic Scholar and OpenAlex were throttled or timed out, and citation expansion failed. Results come from arXiv search plus known seeds, so some follow-ups may be missing and there are no citation counts.
Citation links are inferred from abstracts that name the cited method (e.g., GRPO→DeepSeekMath, Dr. GRPO, DAPO, RLOO); reference lists were not checked directly.
The CISPO quote is cut off mid-word because the abstract text was truncated.

Not verified or included: Kimi k1.5 (abstract read but left out as more of a recipe paper), ProRL, the high-entropy-token paper (2506.01939), Kalman-filter GRPO, and many 2026 GRPO variants for entropy or token-level credit (EP-GRPO, ERPO, SCOPE-RL, BoT-GRPO, COPC).

Off-policy correction blogs (truncated importance sampling, e.g., the 'Your efficient RL framework secretly brings you off-policy RL' post) and length-penalty or efficient-reasoning work were not covered.
No head-to-head results under matched settings were pulled from the full texts; the evaluation-comparability notes rely on the abstracts only.
Search date: 2026-10-08.

answer.summary:
I made 6 of the 8 allowed research calls. Some 2026 papers (λ-GRPO, LUSPO, Balanced Aggregation, the group-std-identity paper, GDPO, the biased-advantage paper) were found through search snippets. I didn't open their full text, so I left their quotes empty rather than guess. For other entries I left the quote empty where I couldn't confirm wording verbatim. The citation links I added are limited to ones I'm confident about. Most come from the papers' own framing (e.g., titles naming earlier methods, or explicit "fixes GSPO" claims), not from checking reference lists.

**The original objective.** GRPO (DeepSeekMath, then scaled up in R1) replaces PPO's learned critic with a group baseline: (reward − group mean) / group std. This advantage is applied to every token, and the loss is averaged per response, then over the group.

**Objective changes: length and normalization bias.**
- Dr. GRPO drops both the per-response length division and the std division.
- DAPO switches to token-level aggregation, and adds clip-higher and dynamic sampling of groups where every response gets the same reward.
- λ-GRPO learns the token weighting instead of fixing it.
- Balanced Aggregation separates the weights of positive- and negative-advantage responses.
- LUSPO fixes the length bias that remains in GSPO.
- The group-std-identity paper and REINFORCE++ (global normalization) reframe or replace per-group std scaling.
- The biased-advantage paper (HA-DW) and GDPO address difficulty bias and multi-reward collapse in group normalization.

**Objective changes: ratio and clipping stability.** GSPO moves to a sequence-level ratio. GMPO uses a geometric-mean aggregation. CISPO clips the detached IS weight so clipped tokens still contribute gradients. SAPO uses soft sigmoid gating. Clip-Cov/KL-Cov and ProRL (KL plus reference resets) target entropy collapse. The KL-design paper fixes GRPO's KL estimator.

**Training-system changes (objective untouched).**
- FP16 precision removes the mismatch between the rollout and training engines.
- TIS corrects for that mismatch with truncated importance sampling.
- AReaL runs rollouts asynchronously and needs staleness-aware off-policy correction.
- The Qwen "Formulation and Practices" paper links the two layers: the token-level surrogate is only valid when mismatch and staleness are small, which is what IS correction, clipping and Routing Replay protect.

**Comparing results.** Reported gains are not comparable across papers. The base models (Qwen2.5-Math vs. general models vs. MoE), prompt sets, context lengths and decoding settings all differ, and so do the metrics (avg@k vs. pass@1, AIME24 vs. AIME25). Dr. GRPO also showed that template and base-model effects can be as large as algorithm effects. ScaleRL is the main matched-compute comparison of these variants. Use it and same-paper ablations, not cross-paper leaderboard numbers.
gaps: I verified only some quotes and citation edges against full text. The 2026 entries rest on search snippets.
No independent, matched-setup benchmark that compares GRPO, Dr. GRPO, DAPO, GSPO, GMPO, CISPO, SAPO and LUSPO on the same base model, data and compute. ScaleRL covers only a subset.

Effects of objective changes and system fixes (FP16, TIS, Routing Replay, asynchrony) are seldom separated. Many 'stability' gains may come from fixing the training–inference mismatch rather than from the objective.
Theory for length bias is fragmented: per-token weighting, positive/negative aggregation and sequence-ratio length normalization are analyzed separately.
Most evidence comes from math with verifiable rewards on Qwen-family models. Code, agentic multi-turn and non-verifiable rewards are under-tested.
Interaction with the group size G, and with filtering out groups where every response got the same reward, is under-studied with respect to normalization bias.
I didn't search for newer 2026 work on off-policy, stale-rollout and MoE-specific group-relative objectives beyond the Qwen and AReaL papers.

answer.summary:
GRPO (DeepSeekMath, scaled up in DeepSeek-R1) replaces PPO's critic with a group baseline: each reward is compared with the mean and std of a group of responses to the same prompt. It keeps PPO's token-level clipped ratio and averages the loss within each response. Later work splits into two kinds of change.

**Objective changes**
- **Length / aggregation bias:** Dr. GRPO removes per-response length normalization and std normalization. DAPO switches to token-level loss aggregation. λ-GRPO learns the token weighting. GFPO filters the group by length or reward per token. A 2026 impossibility result argues no length weighting can be both unbiased and length-invariant.
- **Reward / normalization:** Dr. GRPO argues the std term biases toward very easy or very hard prompts. REINFORCE++ uses batch-level normalization. Tricks-or-Traps' controlled ablations favor group mean with batch std.
- **Stability of the ratio and clipping:** DAPO uses asymmetric Clip-Higher. CISPO clips the importance weights instead of dropping token gradients. GSPO uses a sequence-level ratio, which matters most for MoE. GMPO uses geometric-mean aggregation. Entropy-mechanism work and ProRL add entropy/KL controls.

**Training-system changes**
- DAPO's dynamic sampling and overlong filtering.
- AReaL-style asynchronous, off-policy rollouts.
- Correcting the precision mismatch between rollout and training engines: FP16 instead of BF16, or truncated importance sampling.
- ScaleRL's PipelineRL and FP32 logits.

These system fixes target instability that often gets blamed on the objective. The FP16 paper argues BF16 mismatch is a root cause, and ScaleRL finds aggregation and normalization choices mostly change compute efficiency rather than the performance ceiling.

**Evaluation caution**
Reported AIME numbers are not comparable across these papers. Base models differ (Qwen2.5-Math-7B for Dr. GRPO, Qwen2.5-32B for DAPO, Qwen3 MoE for GSPO, Phi-4-reasoning for GFPO), as do context limits, sampling temperature, and pass@1 vs avg@k. Qwen-Math also responds even to spurious rewards. The Sober Look and pass@k papers show that seed and decoding variance can swamp many claimed gains. The most reliable comparisons are within-paper controlled ablations (Tricks-or-Traps, ScaleRL, the GFPO vs Dr. GRPO comparison).
gaps: Only 8 tool calls were available. Several abstract quotes are left empty rather than risk misquoting (GMPO, ScaleRL, VAPO, REINFORCE++, GPG, entropy mechanism, ProRL, AReaL, the evaluation papers). Their arXiv IDs come from memory and should be checked.
The citation edges are limited to ones supported by retrieved text or a clear direct comparison. Many more edges almost certainly exist but were not verified.
The truncated-importance-sampling work on training-inference mismatch (Yao et al. 2025, blog) and the Ring-1T/IcePop mismatch fixes are not included as papers.
Process-reward and multi-turn/agentic extensions of group-relative RL, plus non-math domains (code, multimodal), are barely covered.
Newer 2026 work beyond the impossibility paper and the optimal-reasoning-length paper (arXiv 2602.09591, not listed) was not searched systematically.
There is no shared benchmark protocol across these methods, so no cross-paper ranking is given.

answer.summary:
I found 25 papers in four groups, all about first-stage retrieval, plus the benchmarks used to evaluate it. Cross-encoder rerankers (e.g., monoBERT) are left out on purpose; they only come up as the expensive baseline that late interaction tries to approximate.

**1. Late interaction (multi-vector)**
- **ColBERT (2020)** keeps one vector per token and scores with MaxSim, so document representations are computed ahead of time instead of running a model on every query-document pair.
- **Follow-ups** reduce its two main costs:
  - *Index size:* ColBERTv2's residual compression (6–10× smaller), ColBERTer's whole-word reduction, token pooling (about 50% smaller with almost no quality loss), and EigenLI's low-rank approximation per document (2026).
  - *Search speed:* PLAID's centroid pruning (up to 7× faster on GPU, 45× on CPU), XTR's token-retrieval objective, MUVERA's reduction to single-vector search, and FLASH-MAXSIM's fused GPU kernel (2026).

**2. Learned sparse retrieval**
- **SPLADE** and its successors (v2, SPLADE++) keep inverted indexes but learn term weights and expansions. Their gains come mostly from borrowing dense-retriever training: distillation and hard negatives.
- **DeepImpact and COIL** are earlier impact-scoring and contextual-inverted-list designs.
- **Seismic** (inverted indexes for approximate search) addresses query processing: learned sparse vectors are distributed very differently from BM25 weights.
- **SLIM and SPLATE** link the two families: they project ColBERT token vectors into a sparse vocabulary space, so ColBERT candidates can come from a standard inverted index.

**3. Dense-vector compression**
- **JPQ** (product quantization trained jointly with the query encoder) and **BPR** (binary codes) shrink DPR-style single-vector indexes; BPR goes from 65GB to 2GB.

**4. Evaluation**
- **MS MARCO** is the in-domain training and evaluation set.
- **BEIR** set the zero-shot comparison across lexical, sparse, dense, late-interaction and reranking systems. Its main finding: late interaction and reranking were most effective but cost more, while sparse and dense models were cheaper but generalized worse.
- **MTEB** widened evaluation to many embedding tasks and languages. **BRIGHT** (2024) shows that models strong on these benchmarks fail on reasoning-heavy queries.
- **DenseOn/LateOn (2026)** trains a dense model and a ColBERT-style model on the same open data and backbone, which makes the dense-versus-late-interaction comparison controlled.

**Overall trade-off:** late interaction is still the most robust zero-shot option but needs compression and pruning to be practical. Learned sparse retrieval is the CPU-friendly option that fits existing inverted-index infrastructure. Compressed dense retrieval sits between the two on memory.

**Citation links:** I only list a citation where the citing paper's abstract names the cited work, or where the cited work is the base model or benchmark being extended or evaluated (e.g., ColBERTv2→ColBERT, SPLATE→PLAID, BEIR→DPR/ColBERT). None came from a citation-graph lookup, because those requests were throttled.
gaps: The citation-graph expansion failed because Semantic Scholar and OpenAlex throttled requests (HTTP 429 and timeouts), so I could not check reference lists. Citation links rest on the abstracts plus well-known build-on relations, and some real links are probably missing (e.g., Seismic→SPLADE, JPQ→ANCE, DeepImpact→ColBERT).
Citation counts were unavailable, so the 'most influential' ranking is my judgment, not counts.

Only arXiv returned search results. Venue-only papers (SIGIR/ECIR) without arXiv versions may be missing, such as the SPLADE efficiency work, uniCOIL, the BM25/LSR query-processing literature and the TREC DL track overviews.

Recent-window coverage (2024-10-08 to 2026-10-08) is thin and mostly late interaction. Recent learned-sparse items I saw but did not include: GPUSparse (arXiv 2606.26441), SPLADE-v3 query-expansion studies, Mistral-SPLADE (Aug 2024, just before the window) and Two-Step SPLADE (Apr 2024).

Left out as out of scope or borderline: cross-encoder rerankers (monoBERT, arXiv 1901.04085), ANCE dense training, multimodal late interaction (ColPali, Video-ColBERT), language-specific BEIR variants (Polish, Dutch, Hindi) and language-specific ColBERTs (Turkish, Italian).
The quote for the Seismic paper ('Efficient Inverted Indexes…') ends mid-word because the retrieved abstract was cut off at that point.
Search date: 2026-10-08. The 2026 arXiv preprints (EigenLI, FLASH-MAXSIM, DenseOn/LateOn) have not been peer-reviewed.

answer.summary:
This review covers first-stage retrieval only. Cross-encoder reranking is excluded except where a paper uses re-rankers as a point of comparison. Several of the efficiency methods (PLAID, SPLATE, XTR, Two-step SPLADE) score candidates in two steps: an approximate pass, then exact scoring with the same retriever. That is still part of first-stage retrieval, not cross-encoder reranking.

**Late interaction.** ColBERT stores one vector per token and scores with MaxSim. That gives high quality, especially out of domain, but makes the index about 10x larger. Later work attacks the cost from several directions:
- Compression: ColBERTv2's residual compression; token pooling (2024); EigenLI's spectral low-rank compression (2026).
- Search engines: PLAID's centroid pruning.
- Simpler or single-vector-compatible pipelines: XTR (scores from retrieved tokens) and MUVERA (fixed dimensional encodings that work with off-the-shelf single-vector search).
- Sparse candidate generation: SPLATE uses a SPLADE-style sparse index to find ColBERT candidates.

**Learned sparse retrieval.** DeepImpact, COIL/uniCOIL and SPLADE (v2, ++ and v3) keep the inverted index and exact matching, and learn term weights and expansions. Their efficiency problem is that learned weights defeat the skipping optimizations designed for BM25. Responses include new index layouts and query processing (Seismic, Two-step SPLADE) and GPU serving (GPUSparse).

**Compressing single-vector dense retrieval.** JPQ and RepCONC train the encoder and product quantization together; BPR adds binary hashing to DPR. All of them beat compressing the vectors after training.

**Evaluation.** MS MARCO and TREC DL are the in-domain standard. BEIR, and later MTEB and the reasoning-heavy BRIGHT, measure zero-shot robustness. Across these benchmarks the trade-off differs by family: late-interaction and SPLADE-family models are more robust zero-shot, while compressed dense retrievers win on memory and latency.

**How the citation links were sourced.** Most links come from the abstracts themselves (for example, PLAID's abstract names ColBERT and ColBERTv2). A few are well-established author lineages (ColBERTv2→ColBERT, SPLADE++→SPLADE) and were not verified against reference lists.
gaps: Semantic Scholar timed out and OpenAlex returned HTTP 429 on 2026-10-08, so the citation expansion failed. Citation links therefore come from what the abstracts say plus well-known author lineages, not from reference lists. Some true links are missing (e.g., RepCONC→JPQ, Seismic→SPLADE, BEIR→ColBERT/DPR are likely but were not verified and are left out).

Coverage of the last two years (2024-10-08 to 2026-10-08) is thin. It relies on arXiv-only search results: EigenLI, GPUSparse, and also FastLane (2601.06389), the SPLADE-v3 query-expansion study (2609.37911), the 'Wacky Weights' dissection (2605.19628) and Diagnosable ColBERT (2604.19566). These were screened but not all are listed, and their influence cannot yet be judged.

Boundary or omitted items, not included: SLIM (2302.06587), ColBERTer (2203.13088), Two-step SPLADE (2404.13357), Mistral-SPLADE (2408.11119), Jina-ColBERT-v2 (2408.16672), Wacky Weights/score-at-a-time (2110.11540), Matryoshka Representation Learning (2205.13147), BRIGHT (2407.12883), and LLM-based dense embedders.
Some papers known to be relevant were not searched or checked at all: doc2query/DeepCT, ANCE/TAS-B dense training, LADR/EMVB, and ANN-index studies (HNSW/DiskANN) for dense retrieval.
No separate benchmark for efficiency reporting (latency or memory measured under fixed hardware) was found. Efficiency claims across papers are not directly comparable.

answer.summary: Efficient learned first-stage retrieval has three main lines. (1) Late interaction (ColBERT): token-level MaxSim gives quality close to a cross-encoder, but at a high index cost. Follow-up work attacks that cost through residual compression (ColBERTv2), faster engines (PLAID, WARP), training changes that drop the gathering stage (XTR), conversion to single-vector search (MUVERA), and fewer or sparser vectors (token pooling, ColBERTSaR, No More K-means). (2) Learned sparse retrieval runs on inverted indexes. It goes from term weighting (DeepCT, COIL) to expansion with regularization (SPLADE, v2, ++, v3). Recent work speeds up query processing over these unusual weight distributions (Seismic, superblock pruning) or scales the encoders to LLMs while keeping indexes small (CSPLADE). (3) Single-vector dense indexes are compressed with PQ trained jointly with the encoder (JPQ). All of these are first-stage retrievers, unlike cross-encoder rerankers such as monoBERT, which score query-document pairs together and cannot be precomputed. Evaluation has moved from MS MARCO and BEIR zero-shot tests to MTEB and MMTEB, and BRIGHT shows that leaderboard gains don't carry over to reasoning-heavy retrieval. Citation links: WARP's, CSPLADE's and ColBERTSaR→PLAID were checked against fetched pages, ColBERTSaR's from its abstract rather than its reference list. The rest come from my knowledge of the papers.
gaps: No common benchmark reports latency, index size and quality together across late-interaction, LSR and compressed dense systems; BEIR, MTEB and BRIGHT report effectiveness only.
There is little evidence on how efficient first-stage retrievers perform on reasoning-intensive queries (BRIGHT) under compression or pruning.
Comparisons between LLM-scale LSR (CSPLADE) and fast LSR engines such as Seismic or superblock pruning are missing; CSPLADE does not cite Seismic.

Most citation links between the foundational papers come from my knowledge rather than reference lists checked in this session, and several abstract quotes were left blank because they couldn't be confirmed within the budget.

I didn't locate or verify 2025-2026 work on the following: compressing single-vector dense indexes beyond JPQ (e.g., Matryoshka or binary embeddings), multilingual or long-document late interaction, and the inference-free LSR paper (arXiv 2505.01452) and the training-free sequence-compression study (arXiv 2603.22434). Search results surfaced the last two, but I didn't confirm their exact titles, so they're excluded.
Some recent efficiency figures (ColBERTSaR, No More K-means, Seismic) come from abstracts, snippets or secondary summaries; full papers weren't checked.

answer.summary:
I found 25 papers across four groups: late-interaction retrieval, learned sparse retrieval, compression of retrieval indexes, and evaluation. All of them do first-stage retrieval, meaning they search the whole corpus from a precomputed index. The one exception is "Passage Re-ranking with BERT" (monoBERT), included only for contrast. It is a cross-encoder that rescores a small candidate set and is not a first-stage method.

Ranking criteria: papers are listed by group in the order above, not strictly strongest-first.

**How the approaches compare**
- **Late interaction (multi-vector).** ColBERT stores one vector per token, which gives strong zero-shot accuracy but very large indexes. The follow-ups attack that cost in different ways:
  - ColBERTv2 compresses the stored vectors (residual compression).
  - PLAID speeds up search by pruning with cluster centroids.
  - XTR changes training so the cheap token-lookup stage alone finds the right documents.
  - MUVERA turns multi-vector search into ordinary single-vector nearest-neighbour search.
  - WARP (SIGIR 2025) combines the XTR and PLAID ideas. It reports 41x lower latency than XTR's own implementation and about 3x faster search than PLAID.
- **Compressing multi-vector indexes.** The main 2024–2025 approaches are token pooling (about 50% smaller indexes) and principled token pruning (Zong & Piwowarski, SIGIR 2025, keeping about 30% of tokens).
- **Learned sparse retrieval.** DeepImpact, uniCOIL and SPLADE through SPLADE++ keep the standard inverted index but learn term weights and query/document expansion. Two current directions:
  - Faster query processing: Seismic, built for SPLADE-style weights that standard pruning (WAND/MaxScore) handles poorly.
  - Scaling to decoder-only LLMs: Mistral-SPLADE and CSPLADE (up to Llama-3.1-8B), which trade encoding cost for effectiveness and a smaller index.
- **Compressing single-vector indexes.** JPQ trains the query encoder together with product quantization so compressed dense indexes lose little accuracy.
- **Evaluation.** The progression runs from MS MARCO (in-domain) to BEIR (zero-shot), then MTEB and MMTEB (multi-task, multilingual, long-document and code). LIMIT (ICLR 2026) proves that a single embedding's dimension limits which sets of top-k documents it can return. That is a theoretical argument for multi-vector and sparse representations.

**Citation links**
- Checked by reading the papers' reference lists: the WARP and CSPLADE edges.
- Not checked against reference lists in this session: all other edges (author lineage, or a follow-up that builds directly on and evaluates against the earlier method).
gaps: The research budget allowed only 8 tool calls. Quotes are left empty wherever I couldn't confirm the abstract text. Only the WARP and CSPLADE citation edges were checked against the papers' reference lists.
CRISP (clustering-aware multi-vector reduction, 2025) and the Voronoi-cell pruning paper (arXiv 2603.09933) turned up in searches but I didn't verify them, so they are not in the list.

There is little 2025–2026 coverage of efficiency-focused evaluation: no shared latency/memory benchmark across dense, sparse and multi-vector systems, and few TREC/BRIGHT-style reasoning-intensive retrieval results for efficient models.
Multilingual and long-document versions of late interaction and SPLADE (e.g., Jina-ColBERT-v2, multilingual SPLADE) and their compression are not covered.
Hybrid sparse+dense combination and graph-based ANN indexes for dense vectors (HNSW, DiskANN, quantization such as RaBitQ) are outside this list.
No head-to-head study under the same hardware and index budget compares LLM-scale learned sparse retrieval (CSPLADE) with compressed multi-vector engines (WARP, MUVERA).

answer.summary:
Search date: 2026-10-08. Over the last 18 months, ML weather forecasting moved from a research claim to operational practice, and its frontier moved from single forecasts to ensembles.

**Deterministic models (2022–2023).** FourCastNet, Pangu-Weather (a 3D transformer), GraphCast (a mesh graph neural network), FuXi and FengWu were trained on ERA5. They were scored with latitude-weighted RMSE and ACC against ECMWF HRES (the single high-resolution forecast), usually through WeatherBench 2, and verified against ERA5 or the operational analyses. They match or beat HRES on most upper-air variables, but their forecasts are blurred.

**Probabilistic ensembles (late 2024 onward).** There are two routes:
- **Diffusion:** GenCast, LaDCast and ArchesWeatherGen generate members with diffusion or flow-matching. GenCast beat ECMWF ENS (the physics ensemble) on most CRPS targets.
- **CRPS training:** a CRPS-type loss produces each member in a single forward pass. This route is now dominant: AIFS-CRPS with its 'almost fair' CRPS, FGN (whose abstract says it beats current state of the art), FourCastNet 3 (8–60× faster than diffusion), U-Cast (matches GenCast and ENS at 1.5° with more than 10× less training compute) and FuXi-ENS.

Ensembles are evaluated against ENS with CRPS, spread/skill ratios, rank histograms, spectra and tropical cyclone track ensembles.

**Pretrained foundation models.** ClimaX, then Aurora (Nature 2025) and Prithvi WxC, are pretrained broadly and fine-tuned for air quality, ocean waves, tropical cyclones and downscaling. Aurora is compared with operational CAMS and wave forecasts. New critiques find, for example, that Aurora's fine-tuned chemistry is only partly physical.

**Operational versus research.**
- Operational: ECMWF AIFS Single from 25 Feb 2025; [AIFS ENS from 1 Jul 2025](https://www.ecmwf.int/en/about/media-centre/news/2025/ecmwfs-ensemble-ai-forecasts-become-operational), run at 31 km against the 9 km IFS ensemble, with ECMWF reporting gains of up to 20% on some measures; both upgraded to v2 on 12 May 2026 ([ECMWF AIFS data page](https://ecmwf.int/en/forecasts/dataset/aifs-machine-learning-data)). DWD AICON since 2 Mar 2026. WindBorne WeatherMesh-3, a commercial system.
- Research only: GenCast, FGN, FourCastNet 3, U-Cast, LaDCast, NeuralGCM, Aardvark and AIFS-DOP.

Operational systems are verified against observations as well as analyses. Most research papers score against ERA5 or HRES-0 on WeatherBench 2, often at coarse resolution (1–1.5°).

**Next frontier.** End-to-end forecasting directly from observations (Aardvark, AIFS-DOP, FuXi Weather) and extension to seasonal time scales (ACE2, GenCast seasonal).
gaps: Semantic Scholar timed out and OpenAlex was throttled (HTTP 429) during the search and the citation expansion. Results lean on arXiv, so citation counts for 2025–26 papers are missing and the citation edges for recent papers are incomplete; only edges from the provider reference lists are reported.
Citation edges to Aurora, Prithvi WxC, AIFS-CRPS, FGN, FourCastNet 3, U-Cast and AICON could not be retrieved, although those papers very likely cite GraphCast, GenCast and AIFS.
Operational dates (AIFS Single 25 Feb 2025, AIFS ENS 1 Jul 2025, v2 upgrade 12 May 2026) come from ECMWF web pages. There is no peer-reviewed AIFS ENS operational paper in the list.
Several items are 2026 arXiv preprints that have not been peer-reviewed (U-Cast, AIFS-DOP, AICON, the Aurora chemistry analysis). Their claims against ECMWF baselines are self-reported.

Not covered or only touched on: GenCast seasonal (arXiv 2509.06457), FuXi Weather data assimilation (2408.05472), Stormer, FengWu-GHR at kilometre scale, regional/limited-area ML models (Diffusion-LAM, CRPS-LAM), NOAA and other national-centre deployments, and NVIDIA's Earth-2 operational use.

Comparisons often mix resolutions (1.5° research models versus 0.25° or 9 km IFS) and verification targets (ERA5 versus operational analysis versus observations), so headline 'beats ECMWF' claims are not directly comparable.

answer.summary:
I found 25 papers. The field moved through three phases.

**Phase 1 (2022–23): deterministic models matched physics-based forecasts.** FourCastNet, Pangu-Weather (a 3D transformer), GraphCast (a graph neural network on a mesh), FengWu, FuXi and Stormer were all trained on ERA5 reanalysis. They were scored against ECMWF's deterministic forecast (IFS HRES) on latitude-weighted RMSE and ACC, mostly through WeatherBench 2. A known caveat is that HRES is scored against its own analysis while the ML models are scored against ERA5.

**Phase 2 (late 2024–2026): probabilistic ensembles.** The baseline became the ECMWF ensemble (IFS ENS), and the main scores became CRPS, spread–skill ratio and extreme-event and tropical-cyclone metrics.
- **Diffusion models:** GenCast (Nature, Dec 2024) beat ENS on about 97% of targets. Follow-ups include ArchesWeatherGen (flow matching), LaDCast (latent diffusion) and parallel-sampling diffusion.
- **CRPS-trained models:** AIFS-CRPS, FGN, FourCastNet 3 and FuXi-ENS generate each ensemble member in one forward pass. That is cheaper than diffusion and reports equal or better skill. The 2026 preprints try to combine the two approaches.

**Operational use vs. research results.**
- **Running operationally:**
  - ECMWF: AIFS Single from Feb 2025; AIFS ENS from 1 July 2025, upgraded to v2 in May 2026 according to ECMWF's dataset page. AIFS ENS runs at 31 km, compared with 9 km for the IFS ensemble, and still depends on physics-based data assimilation for its starting conditions.
  - Deutscher Wetterdienst: AICON since March 2026.
  - WindBorne: WeatherMesh-3 is a commercial operational system; its skill claims are self-reported.
- **Research results:** GenCast, FGN, FourCastNet 3 and Aurora are published research evaluated on past cases (hindcasts) against ERA5 or HRES/ENS. Their companies' production services are outside these papers.

**Phase 3: pretrained foundation models fine-tuned for other tasks.** ClimaX → Prithvi WxC → Aurora (Nature 2025). Aurora was fine-tuned for air quality (compared against CAMS), ocean waves (against ECMWF's wave model) and tropical cyclone tracks (against official forecasts), at a fraction of the compute.

**Alongside these:**
- NeuralGCM couples a differentiable physics core with ML components.
- FuXi Weather assimilates satellite data directly, removing the dependence on ECMWF starting conditions.
- ACE2 extends ML atmosphere models to seasonal forecasts.

Sources: Citation Lens (arXiv, Semantic Scholar), Nature DOI listings (PMC11666454, dare.uva.nl), and ECMWF news (ecmwf.int/en/about/media-centre/news/2025/ecmwfs-ensemble-ai-forecasts-become-operational).
gaps: The citation-graph step (research_expand) failed because Semantic Scholar and OpenAlex were rate-limiting or timing out. Only three citation links are supported by abstract text: AIFS-CRPS→AIFS, FuXi-ENS→GenCast and ArchesWeather→Pangu-Weather. The other five are from my own knowledge of the papers and should be checked.

The GenCast and Aurora Nature DOIs could not be read through Citation Lens. I confirmed them only through web listings, so their entries use the arXiv URL and arXiv abstract quotes. The Nature GenCast version reports 97.2% rather than 97.4%.
No paper found for the operational AIFS ENS v2 (May 2026) or for AIFS Single v1 technical details. The operational dates come from ECMWF news and dataset pages, not from papers.

Missing or unchecked: GraphCast-based operational products (Google WeatherNext), NOAA and other national-service ML pilots, Microsoft's Aurora-based services, Huawei/CMA operational use of Pangu and FuXi, and Prithvi WxC fine-tuning results.

Not covered in depth: concerns about ML models on extremes and out-of-distribution events, physical consistency (blurring, spectra), and station-based verification (e.g., arXiv 2609.10564, TailWeather 2609.12496).
Search date is 2026-10-08. Papers from 2026, such as AICON and the 2609.x preprints, are recent and have little citation history.
