papers.quote: WeatherBench 2 is an update to the global, medium-range (1-14 day) weather forecasting benchmark

papers.title: The rise of data-driven weather forecasting
papers.reason: ECMWF verified Pangu-Weather and other models with its operational scorecards against IFS, initialized from operational analyses.

papers.title: Demystifying Data-Driven Probabilistic Medium-Range Weather Forecasting
papers.reason: NVIDIA (January 2026) shows that a simple scaled latent model works with stochastic-interpolant, diffusion and CRPS training, with significant gains over IFS ENS and GenCast on most variables.

papers.title: End-to-end data-driven weather prediction (Aardvark Weather)
papers.reason: Replaces data assimilation and NWP with a single ML pipeline from raw observations, benchmarked against operational NWP. Published in Nature in 2025.

papers.title: A data-to-forecast machine learning system for global weather (FuXi Weather)
papers.reason: Cycled ML assimilation of satellite observations feeding forecasts, compared with ECMWF HRES. Published in Nature Communications in 2025.

papers.title: GraphDOP: Towards skilful data-driven medium-range weather forecasts learnt and initialised directly from observations
papers.reason: ECMWF research on learning forecasts directly from observations, skipping the reanalysis or analysis initial state.

papers.title: FuXi: A cascade machine learning forecasting system for 15-day global weather forecast
papers.reason: Cascaded Swin-transformer models that extend skillful ML forecasts to 15 days, compared with the ECMWF ensemble mean.
papers.quote: FuXi achieves comparable performance to ECMWF ensemble mean (EM) in 15-day forecasts

papers.title: FengWu: Pushing the Skillful Global Medium-range Weather Forecast beyond 10 Days Lead
papers.reason: A multi-modal transformer with a replay buffer that extends skillful lead times beyond GraphCast's.

papers.title: Scaling transformer neural networks for skillful and reliable medium-range weather forecasting (Stormer)
papers.reason: A plain ViT-style transformer with randomized-dynamics training that matches GraphCast. Published at NeurIPS 2024.

papers.title: Huge Ensembles Part I: Design of Ensemble Weather Forecasts using Spherical Fourier Neural Operators
papers.reason: Uses SFNO with bred vectors and multiple checkpoints to build ensembles of thousands of members for extremes, evaluated against IFS ENS diagnostics.

gaps: Most headline comparisons use ERA5 as both training data and ground truth, and are initialized from reanalysis rather than real-time analyses. This favors ML models over operational IFS, and only ECMWF's own operational-style verification fully removes that advantage.
Little independent, published verification of operational AIFS ENS or WeatherNext 2 in real time. Most evidence comes from developer-authored papers and ECMWF news items.
Extremes, precipitation and record-breaking events outside the training range are still under-evaluated. Many models are scored mainly on Z500, T850 and T2m.
There is no standard benchmark yet for fine-tuned foundation models across Earth-system tasks. Aurora's air-quality, wave and cyclone results each use different baselines.
End-to-end observation-driven systems (Aardvark, GraphDOP, FuXi Weather) still trail IFS on many variables, and how they would be operationalized is unclear.
I could not verify the details of several late-2026 preprints (e.g., arXiv 2608.26822 and 2609.08412) within the search budget.
The citation links listed are well-known references, not a full bibliography crawl, and I verified quotes only for some papers.

papers.title: GraphCast: Learning skillful medium-range global weather forecasting
papers.role: Foundational: deterministic graph neural network (published in Science, 2023)
papers.reason: A mesh GNN trained on ERA5 that beat ECMWF HRES on most WeatherBench-style targets. It is the basis for GenCast, FGN and the AIFS design.
papers.quote: GraphCast significantly outperforms the most accurate operational deterministic systems on 90% of 1380 verification targets

papers.title: Accurate medium-range global weather forecasting with 3D neural networks (Pangu-Weather)
papers.reason: The first ML model reported to beat the operational ECMWF IFS deterministic forecast on reanalysis-based verification.
papers.quote: Pangu-Weather obtains stronger deterministic forecast results on reanalysis data in all tested variables when compared with the world's best NWP system, the operational IFS of ECMWF

papers.title: FourCastNet: A Global Data-driven High-resolution Weather Model using Adaptive Fourier Neural Operators
papers.role: Foundational: an early 0.25° ML global model
papers.reason: The first ML model to run at 0.25°. It matched IFS at short lead times for large-scale variables, which helped start the field.

papers.title: Forecasting Global Weather with Graph Neural Networks
papers.role: Foundational: precursor to the GNN line
papers.reason: Keisler's encoder–processor–decoder GNN on ERA5, which GraphCast and AIFS later scaled up.

papers.title: GenCast: Diffusion-based ensemble forecasting for medium-range weather
papers.role: Key probabilistic shift: diffusion ensemble (Nature, Dec 2024)
papers.reason: A conditional diffusion model whose 0.25° 15-day ensembles beat ECMWF ENS on almost all CRPS/ensemble-mean targets, plus cyclone tracks and extremes. It became the standard ML ensemble benchmark.

papers.title: AIFS -- ECMWF's data-driven forecasting system
papers.role: Operational deterministic system (AIFS Single, operational 25 Feb 2025)
papers.reason: ECMWF's own GNN/transformer model, trained on ERA5 and fine-tuned on operational analyses. It was verified against IFS HRES and later became operational.

papers.title: AIFS-CRPS: Ensemble forecasting using a model trained with a loss function based on the Continuous Ranked Probability Score
papers.role: Key recent work: CRPS-trained ensemble behind the operational AIFS ENS (operational 1 Jul 2025)
papers.reason: Trained on an almost-fair CRPS loss. Its 50-member, 15-day ensembles, started from IFS ENS initial conditions and verified against ECMWF analysis, beat IFS ENS for most variables and lead times.
papers.quote: the almost fair CRPS is introduced because it approximately removes the bias in the score due to finite ensemble size yet avoids a degeneracy of the fair CRPS

papers.title: Skillful joint probabilistic weather forecasting from marginals
papers.role: Key recent work: FGN, the model behind Google's WeatherNext 2
papers.reason: Learned functional perturbations trained on per-gridpoint CRPS. It reports beating GenCast and ECMWF ENS while still capturing joint spatial structure and cyclone tracks.

papers.title: FourCastNet 3: A geometric approach to probabilistic machine-learning weather forecasting at scale
papers.role: Key recent work: spherical CRPS-style ensemble model
papers.reason: A spherical-convolution hidden Markov model with a spectral probabilistic loss. It beats IFS-ENS, comes close to GenCast at 8–60× its speed, and stays calibrated to 60 days.

papers.title: FuXi-ENS: A machine learning model for medium-range ensemble weather forecasting
papers.role: Key recent work: VAE-style ensemble (Science Advances, 2025)
papers.reason: Flow-dependent learned perturbations, trained with a CRPS+KL loss. It reports beating ECMWF ENS on CRPS for 98.1% of 360 combinations.
papers.quote: in the CRPS of 98.1% of 360 variable and forecast lead time combinations

papers.title: A foundation model for the Earth system (Aurora)
papers.role: Key recent work: pretrained foundation model fine-tuned for Earth-system tasks (Nature, May 2025; arXiv 2405.13063)
papers.reason: A 1.3B-parameter model pretrained on more than 1M hours of data and fine-tuned for air quality (vs CAMS), ocean waves, cyclone tracks (vs 7 centres) and 0.1° weather (vs IFS HRES).
papers.quote: a large-scale foundation model trained on more than one million hours of diverse geophysical data

papers.title: Neural General Circulation Models for Weather and Climate
papers.reason: A differentiable dynamical core with learned physics. It is competitive with ECMWF ENS at 1–15 days and runs stably at climate timescales.
papers.quote: NeuralGCM is competitive with machine-learning models for 1-10 day forecasts, and with the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts ensemble prediction for 1-15 day forecasts

papers.title: WeatherBench 2: A benchmark for the next generation of data-driven global weather models
papers.reason: The standard protocol for comparing ML models with IFS HRES/ENS: ERA5 or IFS-analysis truth, RMSE/ACC/CRPS/spread-skill.

papers.reason: Replaces the full NWP pipeline, data assimilation included, by going directly from raw observations. It was compared with operational NWP baselines.

answer.summary:
I ran 8 searches and page fetches. Most abstract quotes are blank because I didn't open those pages. The few I gave come from search snippets, the 2606.02508 abstract, or recall: the GraphCast, Pangu-Weather and NeuralGCM quotes are from memory and should be checked against the abstracts before reuse. Most citation links are based on the well-known reference lists of these papers, not on lists I opened; only the 2026 comparative study's link to AIFS-CRPS was confirmed. ECMWF's 12 May 2026 upgrade to AIFS v2 came from an ECMWF data page, but I did not find a paper describing v2.

What changed:

**1. Deterministic models (2022–2023).** Keisler's GNN, FourCastNet, Pangu-Weather (3D transformer), GraphCast (mesh GNN), FuXi and FengWu showed that models trained on ERA5 could match or beat ECMWF's IFS HRES. Verification used RMSE and anomaly correlation (ACC) against ERA5 or the IFS analysis, mostly following the WeatherBench 2 protocol. Weaknesses were blurry fields at long lead times and no measure of uncertainty.

**2. Probabilistic ensembles (late 2024 onward).** Two families now dominate:
- **Diffusion:** GenCast, and the flow-matching ArchesWeatherGen. GenCast beat ECMWF ENS on most CRPS targets but is expensive to run.
- **CRPS-trained generators:** AIFS-CRPS, FGN/WeatherNext 2, FourCastNet 3 and FuXi-ENS. They inject noise and train directly on a fair or almost-fair CRPS loss. They report matching or beating GenCast and IFS ENS at much lower cost, with sharp, calibrated members.
- **Evaluation:** these use 50-member, 15-day ensembles scored by CRPS, spread-skill ratio, ensemble-mean RMSE, cyclone tracks and extremes. Truth is ERA5 or the operational ECMWF analysis, with forecasts often started from IFS ENS initial conditions.

**3. Foundation models.** Aurora (Nature 2025), Prithvi WxC and the earlier ClimaX pretrain large transformers and fine-tune them for other tasks. Aurora is the strongest case, reporting wins over CAMS for air quality, over numerical wave models, over 7 forecast centres for cyclone tracks, and over IFS HRES at 0.1°.

**4. Hybrids and end-to-end systems.** NeuralGCM pairs a physics dynamical core with learned physics. Aardvark goes straight from raw observations to forecasts without separate data assimilation. Both are research systems.

**Operational vs research:**
- **Operational at ECMWF:** AIFS Single since 25 Feb 2025 and AIFS ENS since 1 Jul 2025 (51 members at about 31 km, versus 9 km for the IFS ensemble), both upgraded to v2 on 12 May 2026. They run alongside IFS rather than replacing it.
- **Production but not an NWP centre's system:** FGN is offered by Google as WeatherNext 2.
- **Research or experimental:** GenCast, FourCastNet 3 and FuXi-ENS (to my knowledge), Aurora (open weights), plus Aardvark and Nested-EAGLE at NOAA.

**Independent checks.** Verification against station observations (Kocsis & Baran, 2026) found raw IFS ENS clearly better than AIFS for 10 m wind; post-processing narrowed the gap. Skill claims made against analyses or reanalyses don't always carry over to verification against observations.
gaps: Most headline claims are verified against ERA5 or the ECMWF analysis, which favours models trained on that same data. There is little independent verification against station observations, and the few studies that exist (e.g. 2606.02508) show IFS still ahead for some surface variables.

Comparisons often run at different resolutions (e.g. AIFS ENS at 31 km vs IFS ENS at 9 km) and with different initial conditions or ensemble sizes, so 'beats ENS' figures are hard to compare across papers.
Almost all operational ML forecasts still depend on physics-based data assimilation (IFS analyses). End-to-end systems like Aardvark and GraphDOP remain research-stage.
Extremes, precipitation and record-breaking events outside the training data remain weak spots. Deterministic models in particular (e.g. Nested-EAGLE) underperform on precipitation amounts.
Foundation-model claims (Aurora, Prithvi WxC) rely on task-specific baselines (CAMS, wave models, cyclone centres). There is no shared benchmark for transfer across Earth-system tasks.
Subseasonal-to-seasonal and climate-scale stability of CRPS-trained models (FourCastNet 3, AIFS-CRPS) is only starting to be tested.
Peer-reviewed papers on the AIFS v2 upgrade (May 2026) and on WeatherNext 2's operational verification were not found within this search budget.

papers.title: Fast Inference from Transformers via Speculative Decoding
papers.reason: Introduced speculative decoding with a rejection-sampling rule that keeps the target model's output distribution exactly; reported 2-3x speedup on T5-XXL.
papers.quote: In this work we introduce speculative decoding - an algorithm to sample from autoregressive models faster without any changes to the outputs, by computing several tokens in parallel.

papers.title: Accelerating Large Language Model Decoding with Speculative Sampling
papers.role: Foundational: exact draft-and-verify (concurrent with Leviathan et al.)
papers.reason: Independently proposed speculative sampling with a modified rejection-sampling scheme that preserves the target distribution; 2-2.5x on Chinchilla 70B.
papers.quote: This is combined with a novel modified rejection sampling scheme which preserves the distribution of the target model within hardware numerics.

papers.title: Blockwise Parallel Decoding for Deep Autoregressive Models
papers.role: Precursor: multi-head prediction + greedy prefix verification
papers.reason: Earliest predict-many-then-verify scheme: extra heads propose tokens, and the model keeps the longest prefix it validates. This is exact for greedy decoding and the ancestor of Medusa-style heads.
papers.quote: we make predictions for multiple time steps in parallel then back off to the longest prefix validated by a scoring model

papers.title: Speculative Decoding: Exploiting Speculative Execution for Accelerating Seq2seq Generation
papers.role: Precursor: draft-then-verify with a separate drafter (approximate/relaxed verification)
papers.reason: First to use the name 'speculative decoding' for a separate drafter plus verifier. Its relaxed verification gives quality 'comparable' to beam search rather than an exact guarantee.
papers.quote: Spec-Drafter -- an independent model specially optimized for efficient and accurate drafting -- and Spec-Verification -- a reliable method for verifying the drafted tokens efficiently in the decoding paradigm.

papers.title: SpecInfer: Accelerating Large Language Model Serving with Tree-based Speculative Inference and Verification
papers.reason: Introduced token-tree speculation, verified in parallel with tree attention, plus multi-step sampling that provably preserves model quality.
papers.quote: The correctness of all candidate token sequences represented by a token tree is verified against the LLM in parallel using a novel tree-based parallel decoding mechanism.

papers.title: SpecTr: Fast Speculative Decoding via Optimal Transport
papers.role: Theory of acceptance: multi-draft exact verification via optimal transport
papers.reason: Recasts acceptance as optimal transport with membership cost, which generalises verification to several drafts while keeping the target distribution.
papers.quote: A subset of the tokens in the draft are accepted (and the rest rejected) based on a statistical method to guarantee that the final output follows the distribution of the large model.

papers.title: Medusa: Simple LLM Inference Acceleration Framework with Multiple Decoding Heads
papers.role: Influential: multi-head draft alternative + tree attention
papers.reason: Replaces the separate draft model with extra decoding heads and tree-based candidate verification. Its typical-acceptance mode is approximate; greedy/rejection modes are exact.
papers.quote: Using a tree-based attention mechanism, Medusa constructs multiple candidate continuations and verifies them simultaneously in each decoding step.

papers.title: EAGLE: Speculative Sampling Requires Rethinking Feature Uncertainty
papers.reason: Drafts autoregressively at the target model's second-to-top-layer feature level, uses a draft tree, and keeps standard lossless verification.
papers.quote: Firstly, autoregression at the feature (second-to-top-layer) level is more straightforward than at the token level.

papers.title: EAGLE-2: Faster Inference of Language Models with Dynamic Draft Trees
papers.reason: Builds draft trees dynamically from the drafter's calibrated confidence. Reports 3.05x-4.26x speedup while keeping the output distribution unchanged.
papers.quote: we propose EAGLE-2, which introduces a new technique of context-aware dynamic draft tree into drafting modeling.

papers.title: EAGLE-3: Scaling up Inference Acceleration of Large Language Models via Training-Time Test
papers.reason: Drops feature prediction for direct token prediction with multi-layer feature fusion, so the drafter improves as training data scales.
papers.quote: we introduce EAGLE-3, which abandons feature prediction in favor of direct token prediction and replaces reliance on top-layer features with multi-layer feature fusion via a technique named training-time test.

papers.title: Hydra: Sequentially-Dependent Draft Heads for Medusa Decoding
papers.reason: Makes Medusa-style heads depend on earlier draft tokens, which raises draft accuracy and acceptance.
papers.quote: In this work, we propose Hydra heads: a sequentially-dependent drop-in replacement for standard draft heads that significantly improves the accuracy of draft head speculation.

papers.title: Sequoia: Scalable, Robust, and Hardware-aware Speculative Decoding
papers.role: Tree-based verification: optimal tree structure + robust exact sampling
papers.reason: Uses dynamic programming to find the optimal token-tree shape, adds a hardware-aware tree optimizer, and introduces a sampling/verification method that stays robust across temperatures.
papers.quote: Sequoia introduces a dynamic programming algorithm to find the optimal tree structure for the speculated tokens.

papers.title: Block Verification Accelerates Speculative Decoding
papers.reason: Shows that token-by-token verification is suboptimal; verifies the whole block jointly with a provably optimal, still lossless rule.
papers.quote: We propose Block Verification, a simple draft verification algorithm that verifies the entire block jointly and provides additional wall-clock speedup.

papers.title: Break the Sequential Dependency of LLM Inference Using Lookahead Decoding
papers.reason: Uses Jacobi-iteration n-gram generation plus verification, with no auxiliary model or data store, and keeps outputs exact.
papers.quote: we introduce Lookahead decoding, an exact, parallel decoding algorithm that accelerates LLM decoding without needing auxiliary models or data stores.

papers.title: Draft & Verify: Lossless Large Language Model Acceleration via Self-Speculative Decoding
papers.reason: Drafts by skipping layers of the target model itself, then verifies with the full model; lossless with no extra model.
papers.quote: We present a novel inference scheme, self-speculative decoding, for accelerating Large Language Models (LLMs) without the need for an auxiliary model.

papers.title: LayerSkip: Enabling Early Exit Inference and Self-Speculative Decoding
papers.reason: Trains models for early exit; early layers draft and the remaining layers verify, sharing compute and KV cache.
papers.quote: Our proposed self-speculative decoding approach has less memory footprint than other speculative decoding approaches and benefits from shared compute and activations of the draft and verification stages.

papers.title: DistillSpec: Improving Speculative Decoding via Knowledge Distillation
papers.role: Drafter alignment for higher acceptance (exact SD; also studies lossy variants)
papers.reason: Uses on-policy knowledge distillation to align the drafter with the target, raising acceptance rates under the standard exact rule.
papers.quote: we propose DistillSpec that uses knowledge distillation to better align the draft model with the target model, before applying SD.

papers.title: Speculative Decoding with Big Little Decoder
papers.reason: The small model generates and the large model intervenes only occasionally to correct it. This trades exactness for speed.
papers.quote: the large model is only invoked occasionally to refine the small model's inaccurate predictions in a non-autoregressive manner.

papers.title: Judge Decoding: Faster Speculative Sampling Requires Going Beyond Model Alignment
papers.reason: Argues that the exact acceptance rule rejects valid tokens, and replaces likelihood alignment with a learned 'judge' acceptance. It gives up exactness for much higher acceptance.
papers.quote: While this approach guarantees to reproduce the target output, it incurs a substantial penalty: many high-quality draft tokens are rejected, even when they represent objectively valid continuations.

papers.title: Faster Cascades via Speculative Decoding
papers.reason: Combines cascade deferral rules with speculative execution and explicitly gives up SD's quality-neutrality guarantee for better cost-quality trade-offs.
papers.quote: we leverage the best of both these approaches by designing new speculative cascading techniques that implement their deferral rule through speculative execution.

papers.title: Nucleus Speculative Decoding: Plausibility-Aware Verification Beyond Exact Distribution
papers.role: Very recent (Oct 2026): relaxed acceptance with fidelity bounds
papers.reason: Accepts any token inside the target's nucleus and characterises the resulting distributional deviation, giving bounded rather than exact correctness.
papers.quote: NSD accepts a draft token if it satisfies the standard acceptance rule or belongs to the target model's nucleus.

papers.title: UniVer: A Unified Perspective for Multi-step and Multi-draft Speculative Decoding
papers.role: Recent (2026): tree verification as conditional optimal transport
papers.reason: Unifies multi-draft (SpecTr-style OT) and multi-step tree verification into a jointly optimised verification rule.
papers.quote: In this paper, we propose a unified perspective that casts tree-based verification as a conditional OT problem.

papers.title: Better & Faster Large Language Models via Multi-token Prediction
papers.reason: Trains n independent output heads on a shared trunk. The heads improve the model and can be reused for self-speculative decoding (as in DeepSeek-V3-style MTP).
papers.quote: we ask the model to predict the following n tokens using n independent output heads, operating on top of a shared model trunk.

papers.title: REST: Retrieval-Based Speculative Decoding
papers.reason: Replaces the draft LM with retrieval from a datastore and verifies the retrieved tokens as a tree; plug-and-play and training-free.
papers.quote: Unlike previous methods that rely on a draft language model for speculative decoding, REST harnesses the power of retrieval to generate draft tokens.

papers.title: SWIFT: On-the-Fly Self-Speculative Decoding for LLM Inference Acceleration
papers.reason: Picks which layers to skip on the fly to build the drafter during inference, keeping lossless verification without extra training.
papers.quote: Speculative decoding (SD) has emerged as a widely used paradigm to accelerate LLM inference without compromising quality.

answer.summary:
I found 25 papers. Three lineages run from the 2018–2023 foundations to work published in 2026.

**Exact (distribution-preserving) methods.** Leviathan et al. (2022/23) and Chen et al. (2023) introduced draft-then-verify with modified rejection sampling, which provably keeps the target model's output distribution. Several later papers keep that guarantee while improving one part of the pipeline:
- **What drafts.** A distilled small model (DistillSpec), the model's own skipped layers or early exits (Draft & Verify, LayerSkip, SWIFT), retrieval (REST), Jacobi n-grams (Lookahead), or feature-level drafters (EAGLE, EAGLE-2, EAGLE-3).
- **How many candidates are checked.** Token trees with tree attention (SpecInfer, Medusa, Sequoia's DP-optimal trees, EAGLE-2's dynamic trees).
- **The acceptance rule itself.** SpecTr treats multi-draft acceptance as optimal transport. Block Verification proves that jointly verifying a block is optimal and never worse than token-by-token. UniVer (2026) casts tree verification as conditional OT.

**Multi-head alternatives.** These remove the separate draft model by adding prediction heads: Stern et al.'s blockwise parallel decoding (greedy-exact), Medusa, Hydra (sequentially dependent heads), and multi-token-prediction pretraining (Gloeckle et al.). These heads are exact under greedy or rejection-sampling verification. Medusa's popular 'typical acceptance' mode, however, is approximate.

**Approximate acceleration.** These methods deliberately relax the correctness guarantee to raise acceptance:
- Xia et al.'s original SpecDec uses relaxed verification and reports quality comparable to beam search.
- BiLD uses fallback/rollback policies.
- Speculative cascades use deferral rules and give up quality-neutrality.
- Judge Decoding uses a learned judge to accept valid tokens that the exact rule would reject.
- Nucleus Speculative Decoding (Oct 2026) accepts any token in the target's nucleus, with derived fidelity bounds.

Overall, exact methods compete on drafter quality and tree shape. Lossy methods compete on how much distribution shift buys extra acceptance length, and recent work increasingly bounds that shift formally.

**Citation links.** I verified these from the arXiv HTML reference lists of EAGLE-3, Judge Decoding, Nucleus SD and Sequoia, plus explicit statements in the EAGLE-2 and Hydra abstracts.
gaps: The Citation Lens expansion failed twice because Semantic Scholar and OpenAlex were rate-limiting (HTTP 429/throttled), and the first search only got results from arXiv plus one Semantic Scholar query. Citation edges therefore come only from 4 reference lists fetched from arXiv HTML pages plus 2 abstract statements. Many true edges are missing (e.g., Medusa→Leviathan, SpecInfer→Leviathan, EAGLE→Medusa).

Sequoia's reference list was read only through about 100k of 134k characters; it cites 'Big little transformer decoder', which I matched to the BiLD paper (arXiv 2302.07863, later retitled). The Judge Decoding→multi-token-prediction edge relies on the fetch tool's note that the paper is in its bibliography.
Medusa's typical-acceptance mode is described as approximate from background knowledge; the abstract I read was truncated before that detail.

Relaxed-verification work cited by Nucleus SD was found but not screened or quoted: Fuzzy Speculative Decoding, Approximate Speculative Decoding, Cactus (constrained acceptance), MARS (margin-aware verification), 'Margins, not windows', and 'Revisiting judge decoding'. These are prime candidates for the approximate-acceleration lane.

Notable omissions: Online Speculative Decoding, SpecExec, TriForce, Kangaroo, PaSS, ReDrafter, Glide with a CaPE, HASS, Falcon, OPT-Tree, PEARL, SpecDec++, block-diffusion drafters (DFlash, DFlare, SpecDiff-2), and the Xia et al. 2024 survey (arXiv 2401.07851), a useful entry point.

Citation counts were unavailable for many 2024–2026 arXiv entries, so influence ranking for recent work is judgment-based. Search date: 2026-10-08; very recent preprints (Oct 2026) are not peer-reviewed.

papers.title: Fast Inference from Transformers via Speculative Decoding
papers.reason: Introduced speculative decoding: a small model drafts tokens, the large model verifies them in parallel, and a rejection-sampling rule keeps the output distribution unchanged.
papers.quote: an algorithm to sample from autoregressive models faster without any changes to the outputs, by computing several tokens in parallel.

papers.title: Accelerating Large Language Model Decoding with Speculative Sampling
papers.role: Foundational (exact draft-and-verify), developed at the same time as Leviathan et al.
papers.reason: Speculative sampling with modified rejection sampling that keeps the target distribution; gave a 2–2.5x speedup on Chinchilla 70B.
papers.quote: a novel modified rejection sampling scheme which preserves the distribution of the target model within hardware numerics.

papers.title: Blockwise Parallel Decoding for Deep Autoregressive Models
papers.reason: Early use of extra heads to predict several future tokens, keeping the longest prefix that the scoring model validates. This is the ancestor of Medusa-style heads.
papers.quote: we make predictions for multiple time steps in parallel then back off to the longest prefix validated by a scoring model.

papers.title: Speculative Decoding: Exploiting Speculative Execution for Accelerating Seq2seq Generation
papers.reason: Early formalization of draft-then-verify with a dedicated drafter. Its verification is relaxed and approximate, with quality judged as comparable to beam search.
papers.quote: Spec-Drafter -- an independent model specially optimized for efficient and accurate drafting -- and Spec-Verification -- a reliable method for verifying the drafted tokens efficiently

papers.title: SpecInfer: Accelerating Large Language Model Serving with Tree-based Speculative Inference and Verification
papers.reason: Arranges drafts into token trees and checks all branches in one pass using tree attention, while provably preserving model quality.
papers.quote: The correctness of all candidate token sequences represented by a token tree is verified against the LLM in parallel using a novel tree-based parallel decoding mechanism.

papers.title: Medusa: Simple LLM Inference Acceleration Framework with Multiple Decoding Heads
papers.role: Key multi-head draft alternative (no separate draft model)
papers.reason: Adds extra decoding heads plus tree attention. Its 'typical acceptance' option is explicitly approximate: the paper says matching the original distribution is 'typically unnecessary'.
papers.quote: In this paper, we present Medusa, an efficient method that augments LLM inference by adding extra decoding heads to predict multiple subsequent tokens in parallel.

papers.title: EAGLE: Speculative Sampling Requires Rethinking Feature Uncertainty
papers.reason: A lightweight drafter runs autoregressively over the target model's hidden features and uses tree drafts, with lossless speculative sampling.

answer.summary:
This list covers 25 papers on speculative decoding as of 2026-10-08. All citation links come from reading the reference lists of four papers: EAGLE-3, Medusa, Judge Decoding and Sequoia. Citation Lens could not supply citation links because Semantic Scholar and OpenAlex were throttled.

**Draft-and-verify.** Leviathan et al. and Chen et al. established the paradigm: a cheap model drafts tokens, the target model scores them in parallel, and a modified rejection-sampling rule guarantees the output follows the target distribution exactly. Two earlier works used the same draft-then-verify idea but are not distribution-exact: Stern et al. (blockwise, greedy prefix acceptance) and Xia et al.'s SpecDec (relaxed verification).

**Exact follow-ups.** Most later exact work keeps that acceptance rule and improves one of three things:
- **The drafter:** DistillSpec (distillation); Draft & Verify and Kangaroo (self-speculative layer skipping or early exit); EAGLE, EAGLE-2 and EAGLE-3 (feature-level drafters); REST and Lookahead (retrieval or n-gram drafts, no draft model); DFlash (parallel diffusion drafting).
- **The structure of the guess:** tree-based verification. SpecInfer introduced token trees checked with tree attention. Sequoia optimizes tree shape. EAGLE-2 makes trees dynamic. SpecTr and Recursive Speculative Decoding extend the exact acceptance rule to multiple drafts or trees via optimal transport and sampling without replacement. RheoSampling (2026) targets stochastic sampling in dynamic trees.
- **Multi-head alternatives:** these drop the separate draft model. Medusa uses extra heads, Hydra makes the heads sequentially dependent, and Gloeckle et al. build multi-token heads into pretraining. Medusa's optional 'typical acceptance' gives up exactness.

**Exact vs. approximate.** Exact methods (Leviathan/Chen, SpecInfer, SpecTr, Sequoia, EAGLE-1/2/3, Lookahead, Kangaroo, Draft & Verify) leave the output distribution unchanged; their speedup is limited by how often drafts are accepted. Approximate methods relax acceptance to get longer accepted runs and accept some loss of fidelity: BiLD's fallback and rollback, Medusa's typical acceptance, Judge Decoding's learned judge, and Nucleus SD's plausibility-based verification. The trend from 2025 to 2026 is two-sided: lossless drafters improve through training-time tricks and parallel or diffusion drafting, while a separate line of work deliberately relaxes verification.
gaps: Citation Lens expansion failed: Semantic Scholar timed out and OpenAlex returned HTTP 429 (throttled), so no graph-based follow-up or recent lane was retrieved. Recent 2025–2026 papers come only from the arXiv keyword search and may miss important work.

Citation edges were verified only for four citing papers (EAGLE-3, Medusa, Judge Decoding, Sequoia), using a small model to read their reference lists. The Medusa and Sequoia pages were read only partly (the first 100,000 characters). Many real edges, such as EAGLE-2 citing SpecInfer or Hydra citing Medusa, are therefore not listed.

For the 2026 papers (Nucleus SD, RheoSampling, DFlash), only one abstract sentence was seen. Their exactness claims, for example whether DFlash or RheoSampling preserve the target distribution, were not checked in the full text.

Notable work was not retrieved or verified: Online Speculative Decoding, SpecExec, multi-draft/block verification theory (e.g., Block Verification, multi-draft optimal acceptance), HASS, Faster Cascades / lossy speculative cascades, MTP use in DeepSeek-V3, and speculative decoding inside serving systems (vLLM, batch settings like TETRIS).

answer.summary: The field grew from blockwise parallel decoding (Stern 2018, greedy prefix check with extra heads) into exact speculative decoding (Leviathan; Chen 2023). In exact speculative decoding, a cheap drafter proposes tokens and the target model accepts them with modified rejection sampling, so the output distribution is provably unchanged. Later work moves on three axes. (1) Drafter design: separate small models aligned by distillation (DistillSpec); self-speculation by layer skipping (Draft&Verify); multi-head alternatives to a draft model (Medusa, Hydra, multi-token prediction); feature-level autoregressive heads (EAGLE, then HASS, then EAGLE-3, the current lossless state of the art at up to 6.5x); and draft-free Jacobi/n-gram methods (Lookahead). (2) Tree-based verification: SpecInfer introduced token trees and tree attention; SpecTr framed multi-candidate verification as optimal transport; Sequoia optimises tree shape; EAGLE-2 grows trees dynamically. (3) Acceptance-rule optimality under the exactness constraint: block verification (Sun et al.), multi-draft linear-program theory (Khisti et al.; Hu et al.), Traversal Verification (sequence-level, leaf-to-root) and Hierarchical Speculative Decoding (provably lossless, +12% over EAGLE-3). These raise accepted length without changing the output distribution. Approximate methods relax that constraint: Medusa's typical acceptance, and Judge Decoding, which trains a judge to accept good-but-misaligned tokens. They give larger speedups (about 9x claimed) but change the output distribution, so quality has to be checked empirically, not guaranteed.

answer.summary:
I found 25 papers in four groups. One group, exact distribution-preserving methods, runs across all three of the others.

**Exact draft-and-verify.** Two concurrent papers founded this line: Leviathan et al. (speculative decoding) and Chen et al. (speculative sampling). A cheap drafter proposes tokens and a modified rejection-sampling rule keeps the target model's distribution exactly. Blockwise Parallel Decoding (2018) came first but is exact only under greedy decoding.

**Ways to draft.** Later work mostly changes where the drafts come from:
- **Separate small model:** the original setup.
- **Extra heads on the target model:** Medusa, Hydra, multi-token-prediction heads (Gloeckle; DeepSeek-V3's MTP).
- **Feature-level drafters:** EAGLE, EAGLE-2, EAGLE-3. EAGLE-3 is the current strong baseline, reporting up to 6.5x speedup.
- **The model drafting for itself:** Draft & Verify, LayerSkip.
- **No drafter at all:** Lookahead decoding.
- **Parallel diffusion drafters (2026):** DFlash.

**Tree-based verification.** SpecInfer, Medusa and EAGLE-2 verify a tree of candidates in one pass using tree attention. A separate line of theory asks how much can be accepted while staying exact:
- SpecTr treats multi-draft verification as optimal transport.
- Sequoia uses sampling without replacement and dynamic-programming tree construction.
- Block Verification and Traversal Verification judge whole sequences instead of single tokens. Both are proven lossless and optimal for a single chain. They raise acceptance length without changing outputs.

**Approximate acceleration.** These methods trade exactness for speed:
- Medusa's optional 'typical acceptance' rule.
- Judge Decoding: a learned judge accepts tokens that are correct but don't match the target, giving up to about 9x speedup.
- AutoJudge: the same idea without human labels.
- Fuzzy Speculative Decoding: accepts based on a tunable divergence threshold.

A 2026 analysis (Revisiting Lossy Verification) finds that these relaxations can quietly change the output distribution and reduce quality. That keeps exact methods the default in serving systems.

**Overall.** In 2025–2026 the exact line gained from better drafters (EAGLE-3, DFlash), better verification (Traversal), and better scheduling (DLoop). The lossy line is aimed at reasoning and task-correctness settings where matching the target distribution exactly isn't required.
gaps: Most citation links come from just two papers I could open (EAGLE-3 and Traversal Verification), plus search snippets for AutoJudge, Fuzzy Speculative Decoding, DFlash and DLoop. Many real citations are missing, for example EAGLE→Medusa and Medusa→SpecInfer.

Several quotes are left empty (EAGLE-3, Block Verification, Judge Decoding, LayerSkip, the survey, LongSpec, DLoop) because I couldn't confirm the exact abstract wording within the 8-call budget. A few quotes (EAGLE-2, Sequoia, Hydra, Lookahead, Draft & Verify) are recalled from memory, not re-checked.
I only saw DLoop (2610.07659) and the lossy-verification analysis (2607.26627) through search snippets or a partial abstract. Their claims and citation lists are unverified.

Not covered: draft-model distillation and alignment (DistillSpec, Online Speculative Decoding, HASS), retrieval-based drafting (REST), dynamic speculation length (SpecDec++), Apple's ReDrafter, speculative cascades, and long-context or KV-sparse self-speculation (TriForce, MagicDec).

Missing: an independent comparison of exact versus lossy methods under realistic batched serving, where speedups shrink as batch size grows, and evidence on how well lossy verifiers generalize to new tasks.

Missing: a systematic study of how multi-draft optimal-transport verification compares with Traversal and Block verification. One 2026 paper (Dynamic Delayed Tree Expansion, 2602.16994) touches on this but isn't on the list.

papers.title: Gated Linear Attention Transformers with Hardware-Efficient Training
papers.reason: An I/O-aware chunkwise algorithm plus data-dependent gates made linear attention competitive in both speed and quality.
papers.quote: The resulting implementation, dubbed FLASHLINEARATTENTION, is faster than FLASHATTENTION-2 (Dao, 2023) as a standalone layer even on short sequence lengths (e.g., 1K).

papers.title: Parallelizing Linear Transformers with the Delta Rule over Sequence Length
papers.reason: A Householder-product (WY) algorithm made delta-rule training parallel over the sequence, which allowed DeltaNet to scale. It improves associative recall over additive linear attention.
papers.quote: exploits a memory-efficient representation for computing products of Householder matrices. This algorithm allows us to scale up DeltaNet to standard language modeling settings.

papers.title: Unlocking State-Tracking in Linear RNNs Through Negative Eigenvalues
papers.role: Key theory/design result on state tracking (ICLR 2025)
papers.reason: Shows that limiting transition eigenvalues to [0,1] rules out parity. Widening the range to negative eigenvalues fixes this for Mamba and DeltaNet.
papers.quote: We prove that finite precision LRNNs with state-transition matrices having only positive eigenvalues cannot solve parity, while non-triangular matrices are needed to count modulo $3$.

papers.title: DeltaProduct: Improving State-Tracking in Linear RNNs via Householder Products
papers.role: State-tracking follow-up to DeltaNet (2025; venue not verified)
papers.reason: Takes several delta (online gradient descent) steps per token, i.e. products of Householder matrices. This lets it trade compute for expressivity in state tracking.
papers.quote: Building on the interpretation of DeltaNet's recurrence as performing one step of online gradient descent per token on an associative recall loss, we introduce DeltaProduct, which instead takes multiple ($n_h$) steps per token.

papers.title: RWKV-7 "Goose" with Expressive Dynamic State Evolution
papers.role: Generalized delta-rule RNN (2025; venue not verified)
papers.reason: A delta rule with vector-valued gates and in-context learning rates. The authors claim it recognizes all regular languages and therefore does state tracking that TC0 Transformers cannot.
papers.quote: We show that RWKV-7 can perform state tracking and recognize all regular languages, while retaining parallelizability of training.

papers.title: Gated DeltaNet-2: Decoupling Erase and Write in Linear Attention
papers.reason: Splits the single scalar delta gate into separate channel-wise erase and write gates. It generalizes both GDN and KDA.
papers.quote: Gated Delta Rule-2 separates these roles with a channel-wise erase gate b_t and a channel-wise write gate w_t, reducing to KDA when both gates collap

papers.title: MiniMax-01: Scaling Foundation Models with Lightning Attention
papers.reason: The first frontier-scale (456B MoE) model mostly built from linear 'lightning' attention interleaved with softmax layers, with 1M-token training context.
papers.quote: The context window of MiniMax-Text-01 can reach up to 1 million tokens during training and extrapolate to 4 million tokens during inference at an affordable cost.

papers.title: MiniMax-M1: Scaling Test-Time Compute Efficiently with Lightning Attention
papers.reason: Shows that a hybrid with linear attention reduces the cost of long RL rollouts and test-time compute.
papers.quote: the lightning attention mechanism in MiniMax-M1 enables efficient scaling of test-time compute.

papers.title: Nemotron-H: A Family of Accurate and Efficient Hybrid Mamba-Transformer Models
papers.reason: Replaces most attention layers with Mamba-2. It matches Qwen-2.5/Llama-3.1 accuracy with up to 3x faster inference.
papers.quote: we replace the majority of self-attention layers in the common Transformer model architecture with Mamba layers that perform constant computation and require constant memory per generated token.

papers.title: Hunyuan-TurboS: Advancing Large Language Models through Mamba-Transformer Synergy and Adaptive Chain-of-Thought
papers.reason: A 560B-total/56B-active Mamba2+GQA+MoE model deployed in industry, with a 256K context.
papers.quote: it supports a 256K context length and is the first industry-deployed large-scale Mamba model.

papers.title: Falcon-H1: A Family of Hybrid-Head Language Models Redefining Efficiency and Performance
papers.role: Production hybrid with parallel heads (technical report, 2025)
papers.reason: Runs attention and SSM in parallel within each layer instead of interleaving layers. Released at 0.5B–34B.
papers.quote: Falcon-H1 adopts a parallel hybrid approach that combines Transformer-based attention with State Space Models (SSMs), known for superior long-context memory and computational efficiency.

papers.title: A Systematic Analysis of Hybrid Linear Attention
papers.reason: Trains 72 models covering 6 linear-attention variants at 5 hybrid ratios. Finds that the best standalone linear model is not necessarily the best one in a hybrid.
papers.quote: Benchmarking on standard language modeling and recall tasks reveals that superior standalone linear models do not necessarily excel in hybrids.

papers.title: Hymba: A Hybrid-head Architecture for Small Language Models
papers.reason: Parallel attention and SSM heads plus meta tokens, cross-layer KV sharing and partial SWA to shrink the cache.
papers.quote: Attention heads provide high-resolution recall, while SSM heads enable efficient context summarization.

papers.title: Samba: Simple Hybrid State Space Models for Efficient Unlimited Context Language Modeling
papers.reason: A layerwise Mamba + sliding-window-attention hybrid that extrapolates to 256K with perfect passkey recall.
papers.quote: Samba selectively compresses a given sequence into recurrent hidden states while still maintaining the ability to precisely recall recent memories with the attention mechanism.

papers.title: Log-Linear Attention
papers.reason: Replaces the fixed-size state with a logarithmically growing set of states. This keeps matmul-rich training while easing the recall limit of a fixed state.
papers.quote: Log-linear attention replaces the fixed-size hidden state with a logarithmically growing set of hidden states.

papers.title: Simple linear attention language models balance the recall-throughput tradeoff
papers.role: Foundation for the recall/state-size tradeoff (Based, ICML 2024)
papers.reason: Identifies the state-size versus recall tradeoff that motivates both hybrids and delta-rule designs.
papers.quote: we identify a key tradeoff between a model's state size and recall ability.

papers.title: Jamba: A Hybrid Transformer-Mamba Language Model
papers.reason: The first large interleaved Transformer–Mamba–MoE model and the template for later layer-ratio hybrids.
papers.quote: Jamba interleaves blocks of Transformer and Mamba layers, enjoying the benefits of both model families.

papers.title: Jamba-1.5: Hybrid Transformer-Mamba Models at Scale
papers.reason: Scales the hybrid to 94B active parameters with a 256K effective context and ExpertsInt8 for cheaper serving.
papers.quote: have an effective context length of 256K tokens, the largest amongst open-weight models.

papers.title: Comba: Improving Bilinear RNNs with Closed-loop Control
papers.reason: Groups delta-rule models as 'bilinear RNNs' and adds feedback corrections with a scalar-plus-low-rank transition.
papers.quote: these models introduce interactions between the recurrent state and the key vector, structurally resembling bilinear systems.

papers.title: PaTH Attention: Position Encoding via Accumulating Householder Transformations
papers.role: Delta-rule ideas transferred to softmax attention layers in hybrids (2025)
papers.reason: Uses data-dependent Householder products, the DeltaNet machinery, as position encoding. This improves the state tracking of the full-attention layers.
papers.quote: PaTH, a flexible data-dependent position encoding scheme based on accumulated products of Householder(like) transformations, where each transformation is data-dependent

answer.summary:
Search date: 2026-10-08. Over 2025–26 the field converged on a recipe. **Peer-reviewed results** (ICLR/ICML/NeurIPS: Mamba-2, GLA, DeltaNet, Gated DeltaNet, Negative Eigenvalues, Samba, Hymba, Based, Mamba-3 at ICLR 2026) set up the mechanisms. **Production-scale evidence** comes almost entirely from non-peer-reviewed technical reports and blog posts: MiniMax-01/M1, Nemotron-H, Hunyuan-TurboS, Falcon-H1, Jamba-1.5, Kimi Linear, and Qwen3-Next/Qwen3.5, which has no arXiv report.

**Recall:** fixed-state models lose recall as state size shrinks (Based). Two changes helped. (a) Delta-rule writes (DeltaNet, then Gated DeltaNet, KDA and GDN-2) overwrite associations instead of adding to them, and gating lets the model erase quickly. Finer channel-wise gates (KDA) and decoupled erase/write gates (GDN-2) refine this further. (b) Keeping a minority of full-attention layers: about 1 in 4 (Qwen3-Next/3.5 3:1 GDN:attention; Kimi Linear KDA:MLA). Nemotron-H keeps ~8% attention layers and MiniMax keeps 1 softmax layer per 7 lightning-attention layers; both ratios come from my memory, not from the sources read here. The systematic hybrid study warns that the best standalone linear layer is not necessarily the best one inside a hybrid.

**State tracking:** allowing negative or complex eigenvalues in the transition matrix (Grazzi et al.; Mamba-3's complex/RoPE-like update) and non-diagonal Householder transitions (DeltaNet, DeltaProduct, RWKV-7) make parity and modular counting solvable. PaTH carries the same idea into the attention layers.

**Inference cost:** the gains come from constant-memory decode in most layers plus a shrunken KV cache in the rest: MLA in Kimi Linear, GQA in Hunyuan, SWA and KV sharing in Hymba. Nemotron-H reports up to 3x throughput and Kimi Linear reports large KV-cache and decode savings at 1M context. Kernel work makes training competitive: chunkwise/WY/DPLR algorithms and Mamba-3's MIMO, which adds expressivity without decode latency.

**Selective SSMs vs delta rule:** Mamba-2-style SSM hybrids (Nemotron-H, Hunyuan-TurboS, Falcon-H1, Jamba) dominated early 2025. Gated-delta hybrids (Qwen3-Next/3.5, Kimi Linear) became the leading open design by late 2025–26. Mamba-3 is the SSM line's answer, adding complex states and MIMO.
gaps: Citation Lens expansion failed: Semantic Scholar and OpenAlex were throttled (HTTP 429/timeouts). The citation edges listed are therefore not from tool-verified reference lists. They are limited to cases where the citing abstract names the cited work, or where the dependency is a well-known direct one (e.g., Gated DeltaNet builds on Mamba-2 and DeltaNet). Treat them as high-confidence but unverified.

Qwen3-Next / Qwen3.5 (Gated DeltaNet + gated attention, 3:1) have no arXiv technical report that I could find. Their details come from secondary blogs (Raschka, Kaitchup, mlabonne), so they are not listed as papers.

Peer-review status is partly unverified. Mamba-3 is at ICLR 2026 per the arXiv/ICLR listing. The venues for DeltaProduct, RWKV-7, Log-Linear Attention, PaTH and Titans were not checked in this session. The Jamba venue was not checked either. GDN-2, Comba and the Systematic Hybrid analysis appear to be preprints.
Mamba-3 quote left empty: I did not read its abstract directly. Its claims (complex-valued state, MIMO, half the state size) come from search snippets of the arXiv/ICLR pages.

Omitted or borderline work: Titans (2501.00663; test-time-learned memory, adjacent to the delta rule), Gated KalmaNet, Preconditioned DeltaNet and Complex KDA (all 2025–26 preprints). Also omitted are serving/quantization work for GDN/KDA hybrids (DASC, LeapQuant, STEPQuant), xLSTM-7B, Jet-Nemotron/PostNAS, MiniMax-M2's reported return to full attention, IBM Granite 4.0 and Nemotron Nano 2. None of these were verified this session.

There are no independent, peer-reviewed head-to-head comparisons of production hybrids. Claims such as 'outperforms full attention' (Kimi Linear) and '3x faster' (Nemotron-H) are self-reported in technical reports.

answer.summary:
Linear-time language models in the last 18 months fall into three linked lines of work, plus hybrids that combine them with attention.

**1. Selective SSMs (Mamba → Mamba-2 → Mamba-3).**
- Mamba made the recurrence depend on the input.
- Mamba-2 recast it as structured state-space duality (SSD), a form of scalar-gated linear attention, which made training 2–8× faster.
- Mamba-3 (2026, arXiv) changes the design for inference first: a richer discretized recurrence, complex-valued states for state tracking, and multi-input multi-output (MIMO) updates for decoding efficiency.

**2. Gated linear attention and delta-rule recurrences (GLA → DeltaNet → Gated DeltaNet → KDA / Gated DeltaNet-2, RWKV-7).**
- Recall improved mainly by replacing purely additive or decaying writes with delta-rule overwrites. These subtract the old value stored under a key before writing the new one.
- Gated DeltaNet combines this with decay gating so the model can also erase memory quickly.
- Kimi Delta Attention (KDA) refines the gate to per-channel; Gated DeltaNet-2 separates the erase gate from the write gate.
- Hardware-efficient chunkwise algorithms (FlashLinearAttention, WY/Householder representations, the constrained DPLR kernel in KDA) made these layers practical at scale.

**3. State tracking (mostly theory-driven).**
- Grazzi et al. (ICLR 2025) proved that transition matrices with only positive eigenvalues cannot solve parity. Extending the eigenvalue range to [−1, 1] fixes this.
- DeltaProduct takes several Householder (delta-rule) steps per token.
- RWKV-7 generalizes the delta rule and claims recognition of all regular languages.
- Mamba-3 uses complex-valued states for the same purpose.

**4. Hybrids at production scale.**
- Production systems now keep a small fraction of global attention for exact retrieval:
  - Jamba: Mamba plus attention plus MoE.
  - MiniMax-01: lightning attention with periodic softmax layers.
  - Nemotron-H: mostly Mamba-2, up to 3× faster inference.
  - Falcon-H1: attention and SSM heads in parallel within each layer.
  - Kimi Linear: KDA interleaved with MLA, reported to beat full attention under matched training.
  - Qwen3-Next: Gated DeltaNet plus gated attention.
- Controlled studies (the systematic hybrid analysis, NVIDIA's empirical Mamba study, Samba) find:
  - Recall depends mostly on how many attention layers the hybrid keeps and on the choice of linear layer, especially gating and the delta rule.
  - The best standalone linear layer is not necessarily the best one inside a hybrid.
- Inference cost drops because KV-cache memory and per-token compute are constant in the linear layers.
- Log-linear attention, sparse or exact memory add-ons (Raven, HOLA) and distillation into hybrids (Mamba-in-the-Llama, HALO) are the newest ways to recover recall without fully paying the cost of attention.

**Peer-reviewed vs. technical reports.**
- Peer-reviewed:
  - ICML 2024: Mamba-2, GLA.
  - NeurIPS 2024: DeltaNet.
  - ICLR 2025: Gated DeltaNet, negative-eigenvalues paper, Samba.
  - Mamba itself appeared at COLM 2024.
- Technical reports or preprints: Jamba (2024 report), MiniMax-01, Nemotron-H, Falcon-H1, Kimi Linear, RWKV-7, and the 2026 preprints.
- The claims about production models come from vendor reports, not independent replication.
gaps: Semantic Scholar timed out and OpenAlex rate-limited (HTTP 429) during both the search and the expansion. Some citation edges come from incomplete reference lists. I dropped one implausible edge where the June 2024 DeltaNet paper appears to cite the December 2024 Gated DeltaNet paper.

Venue and acceptance status for DeltaProduct, Gated Attention, Gated Slot Attention, Mamba-in-the-Llama, Jamba (ICLR 2025 version), Mamba-3 and Log-Linear Attention is from memory and was not verified with these tools.
Qwen3-Next and Qwen3.5 (Gated DeltaNet + gated attention hybrids) have no dedicated arXiv paper in my results, so they are covered only indirectly via the Gated Attention paper.

Not retrieved or screened: Hunyuan-TurboS, MiniMax-M1, Jamba-1.5 report, Zamba2, IBM Granite 4.0 hybrids, xLSTM 7B, Titans / test-time-training memories, and the theory of SSM recall limits (e.g., 'Repeat After Me', the Zoology/Based recall papers).

Head-to-head comparisons of production hybrids (recall at 128K+, state-tracking benchmarks, decoding throughput) are not independently replicated. Most efficiency numbers are self-reported in vendor technical reports.
Recent 2026 preprints (Gated DeltaNet-2, Raven, Complex KDA, Kalman Linear Attention, Sparse Delta Memory) have few citations and no peer review yet.
Search run on 2026-10-08 using arXiv plus partial Semantic Scholar citation data; I used 3 of the 8 allowed tool calls.

papers.reason: Showed a Pareto frontier between recurrent state size and recall. Mixing linear and sliding-window attention (BASED) is an early form of the hybrid recipe.

papers.title: Repeat After Me: Transformers are Better than State Space Models at Copying
papers.reason: Proved and showed empirically that fixed-state models cannot copy long strings. This is the core reason production hybrids keep some full-attention layers.
papers.quote: transformers can copy strings of exponential length while GSSMs are limited by their fixed-size latent state

papers.title: Mamba-3: Improved Sequence Modeling using State Space Principles
papers.reason: Adds exponential-trapezoidal discretization, complex-valued states for state tracking, and a MIMO update. Reported: about 1.8 points better than Gated DeltaNet at 1.5B scale, and Mamba-2 perplexity with half the state size.

papers.title: Kimi Linear: An Expressive, Efficient Attention Architecture
papers.reason: Kimi Delta Attention adds channel-wise gating to Gated DeltaNet, interleaved 3:1 with NoPE MLA. Reports up to 75% less KV cache and up to 6x decoding throughput at 1M context.
papers.quote: outperforms full attention under fair comparisons across various scenarios

papers.title: Gated DeltaNet-2: Decoupling Erase and Write in Linear Attention
papers.reason: Splits the single gate into separate channel-wise erase and write gates, generalizing both Gated DeltaNet and KDA. Gains are largest on RULER multi-key retrieval against Mamba-3 and KDA.
papers.quote: replaces the unbounded cache of softmax attention with a fixed-size recurrent state

papers.title: RWKV-7 "Goose" with Expressive Dynamic State Evolution
papers.role: Generalized delta-rule RNN, in window. Preprint/report
papers.reason: Uses a generalized delta rule with vector-valued gating and in-context learning rates. It claims state tracking beyond TC^0 with a constant-memory recurrence.
papers.quote: generalized formulation of the delta rule with vector-valued gating and in-context learning rates

papers.title: DeltaProduct: Improving State-Tracking in Linear RNNs via Householder Products
papers.role: State-tracking follow-up, in window. Peer-reviewed: NeurIPS 2025 (I believe; check)
papers.reason: Takes several delta steps per token (a product of Householder matrices). This lets you trade compute for more expressive transitions and better group-word state tracking.

papers.title: Jamba: A Hybrid Transformer-Mamba Language Model
papers.role: First large production SSM-attention hybrid. Peer-reviewed: ICLR 2025
papers.reason: Established the interleaving recipe at scale: mostly Mamba layers with about 1 attention layer in 8, plus MoE, giving a small KV cache at 256K context.
papers.quote: Jamba interleaves blocks of Transformer and Mamba layers, enjoying the benefits of both model families.

papers.title: An Empirical Study of Mamba-based Language Models
papers.reason: Compared pure Mamba, Mamba-2, Transformer and hybrids at 8B on 3.5T tokens. Pure SSMs lagged on recall and in-context learning, while a hybrid with about 8% attention beat the Transformer.

papers.role: Production hybrid, in window. Technical report

papers.quote: hybrid Mamba-Transformer models designed to reduce inference cost for a given accuracy level

papers.reason: Combines Mamba, attention and MoE (LatentMoE), with NVFP4 training and MTP, up to 1M context. Super (120B-A12B) and Ultra (550B-A55B) followed in 2026.

papers.reason: First very large model to put lightning (linear) attention in most layers, with softmax attention every 8th layer, for multi-million-token context.
papers.quote: The core of MiniMax-01 lies in lightning attention and its efficient scaling.

papers.title: MiniMax-M1: Scaling Test-Time Compute Efficiently with Lightning Attention
papers.role: Production hybrid reasoning model. Technical report

papers.quote: the world's first open-weight, large-scale hybrid-attention reasoning model

papers.role: Fully open controlled hybrid, 2026. Technical report
papers.reason: Swaps Olmo 3's sliding-window layers for Gated DeltaNet (3 linear : 1 attention). Reports better data efficiency and argues hybrids can express tasks beyond both parent architectures.
papers.quote: with the sliding window layers replaced by Gated DeltaNet layers

papers.role: Full-attention component of the Qwen3-Next/3.5 hybrids. Peer-reviewed: NeurIPS 2025
papers.reason: A sigmoid output gate on SDPA removes attention sinks and helps long-context extrapolation. Qwen pairs this gated attention 1:3 with Gated DeltaNet.
papers.quote: applying a head-specific sigmoid gate after the Scaled Dot-Product Attention (SDPA) consistently improves performance

papers.title: Log-Linear Attention
papers.role: Middle ground between linear and quadratic. Preprint (venue unverified)
papers.reason: Replaces the fixed-size state with a logarithmically growing set of Fenwick-tree states, applied to Mamba-2 and Gated DeltaNet to improve recall at O(log T) memory.
papers.quote: Log-linear attention replaces the fixed-size hidden state with a logarithmically growing set of hidden states.

papers.title: Falcon-H1: A Family of Hybrid-Head Language Models Redefining Efficiency and Performance
papers.role: Production hybrid, parallel heads. Technical report

papers.quote: parallel hybrid approach that combines Transformer-based attention with State Space Models (SSMs)

answer.summary:
The field has converged on one recurrence: a fixed-size matrix memory S_t = A_t S_{t-1} + write_t. The approaches differ mainly in the transition A_t.

**1. Selective SSMs (Mamba → Mamba-2 → Mamba-3)**
- Mamba-2 uses a scalar per-head decay. That makes training fast (via SSD), but recall and state tracking are weak.
- Mamba-3 (ICLR 2026) gets more out of the same state with three changes: trapezoidal discretization, complex-valued (rotational) states for state tracking, and MIMO updates. It reports matching Mamba-2 perplexity with half the state.

**2. Gated linear attention (GLA, lightning attention)**
- This line added data-dependent, channel-wise decay and the chunkwise kernels that made training efficient.

**3. Delta-rule recurrences (DeltaNet → Gated DeltaNet → KDA → Gated DeltaNet-2; RWKV-7 and DeltaProduct are relatives)**
- These replace pure decay with an error-correcting erase-then-write update: a rank-1 Householder-like transition.
- This gave the largest recall gains on MQAR- and NIAH-style tests (MQAR = multi-query associative recall; NIAH = needle in a haystack).
- Allowing negative eigenvalues (ICLR 2025) or products of Householder matrices (DeltaProduct) adds provable state tracking, e.g. parity and permutation groups.
- In 2025–26 the refinements are finer gating: KDA's channel-wise gates, and Gated DeltaNet-2 decoupling the erase and write gates. These mainly improve long-context multi-key retrieval.

**4. Hybrids**
- Theory (Repeat After Me, Zoology/BASED) and controlled studies (NVIDIA's 8B study, Olmo Hybrid) agree that a fixed state cannot do unbounded copying or recall. So production models keep a small fraction of full attention:
  - Jamba: about 1 attention layer in 8.
  - MiniMax-01/M1: 1 in 8.
  - Nemotron-H and Nemotron 3: about 8% attention, with Mamba-2 and MoE.
  - Kimi Linear: 3 KDA layers to 1 MLA layer.
  - Qwen3-Next/Qwen3.5: 3 Gated DeltaNet layers to 1 gated-attention layer.
  - Olmo Hybrid: 3 to 1.
  - Falcon-H1 instead runs attention and SSM heads in parallel within each layer.
- The trend is moving from Mamba layers to gated delta-rule layers as the linear component (Qwen, Kimi, AI2). NVIDIA stays with Mamba.
- Inference gains come from shrinking the KV cache: Kimi reports 75% less and up to 6x decoding throughput at 1M context; Nemotron-H reports about 3x throughput.

**Peer-reviewed vs. technical reports**
- Peer-reviewed: the layer-level and theory papers (Mamba-2, GLA, DeltaNet, Gated DeltaNet, negative eigenvalues, Illusion of State, Zoology, BASED, Repeat After Me, Jamba, Gated Attention, Mamba-3).
- Self-reported technical reports: nearly all production-scale results (Kimi Linear, MiniMax-01/M1, Nemotron-H/3, Falcon-H1, Olmo Hybrid, NVIDIA's empirical study). Gated DeltaNet-2 is a preprint.
gaps: Qwen3-Next and Qwen3.5 (Gated DeltaNet + gated attention at 3:1) are described only in blogs and model cards; I found no arXiv technical report, so their ablations can't be checked.

Production hybrid claims (KV savings, throughput, 'beats full attention') come from self-reported technical reports. They lack independent replication at matched data and compute, and use different benchmarks and context lengths.

There is no peer-reviewed, controlled comparison at more than 7B parameters of Mamba-2/3 against Gated DeltaNet/KDA as the linear layer inside a hybrid. The choice of layer ratio and placement (interleaved vs. parallel heads, NoPE in the attention layers) is mostly heuristic.

The state-tracking gains (negative eigenvalues, complex states, DeltaProduct) are shown on synthetic group-word tasks. Evidence that they improve real reasoning or code at production scale is thin; Olmo Hybrid makes theoretical claims.

Long-context recall beyond the training length (RULER at 1M) and length extrapolation of the linear layers are still weak points. Fixes such as log-linear attention and SpectralShift (arXiv 2609.14320, not verified) are recent preprints.

Peer-review status for several papers was not checked in this session: RWKV-7, DeltaProduct, Log-Linear Attention and Falcon-H1. Several September 2026 arXiv preprints surfaced in search (e.g. 'What Attention Recalls and Recurrence Controls in Hybrid Language Models', 'Complex KDA') but I did not open them, so they are excluded.
The tool budget (6 calls) limited quote checking; I left quotes empty where I couldn't confirm the exact abstract wording.

answer.summary:
Over the last 18 months, three families of linear-time layers have converged on one recipe: a matrix-valued recurrent state, updated through gating and a delta-rule (error-correcting) write, interleaved with a small fraction of full attention.

**Selective SSMs (Mamba → Mamba-2 → Mamba-3).**
- Mamba-2's SSD framework showed these layers are scalar-decay gated linear attention. That made chunked matmul training possible.
- Mamba-3 (ICLR 2026) goes after state tracking with complex-valued states and gets more quality from the same decode cost using MIMO updates.

**Gated linear attention to delta rule.**
- Plain decay gating (GLA, Lightning, Mamba-2) is cheap but recalls poorly: it can only fade memory, not overwrite a specific key.
- The delta rule (DeltaNet, NeurIPS 2024) supports targeted overwrites. Gated DeltaNet (ICLR 2025) adds decay on top, giving the best mix of recall and length extrapolation.
- Later refinements make the gates finer-grained: channel-wise gating in KDA (Kimi Linear) and decoupled erase/write gates in Gated DeltaNet-2 (2026 technical report).

**State tracking.**
- The peer-reviewed theory says diagonal, positive-eigenvalue recurrences cannot track state (Illusion of State; Negative Eigenvalues).
- The fixes are: eigenvalues extended to [-1,1], Householder products (DeltaProduct), RWKV-7's generalized delta rule, and complex states (Mamba-3).

**Production hybrids, 2025-26.**
- Most keep 1 attention layer per 3-8 linear layers:
  - MiniMax-01: Lightning attention, 7:1.
  - Nemotron-H and Nemotron 3: Mamba-2, with about 8% attention.
  - Kimi Linear: KDA plus MLA, reportedly 3:1.
  - Qwen3-Next/Qwen3.5: Gated DeltaNet with about 25% full attention. This comes from third-party analysis; there is no official arXiv report.
  - Falcon-H1: parallel attention and Mamba heads within a layer.
- Inference gains come from KV-cache reduction (up to 75%) and a constant per-token state. The reported decode speedups are about 3x for Nemotron-H and up to 6x at 1M context for Kimi Linear.
- Mechanistic studies (2026) agree that exact retrieval lives in the attention KV cache, while the recurrent state controls style and language. That is why some attention is still kept.

**Peer-reviewed vs technical reports.**
- Peer-reviewed: Mamba, Mamba-2, GLA, DeltaNet, Gated DeltaNet, Negative Eigenvalues, Illusion of State, Zoology, Based, Mamba-3, DeltaProduct (venue from memory), and Findings of EMNLP 2026 for the hybrid-mechanism study.
- Technical reports or preprints: all production-model papers (Jamba, MiniMax-01, Nemotron-H, Nemotron 3, Falcon-H1, Kimi Linear), RWKV-7, Gated DeltaNet-2, and the 2606.15378 hybrid analysis.
- The headline claims that hybrids "beat full attention" come only from the technical reports, and only under the vendors' own matched-recipe comparisons.
gaps: There is no official arXiv technical report for Qwen3-Next/Qwen3.5. Its layer ratio and gating details are known only from blog posts and third-party analysis.
MiniMax-M2 reverted from hybrid to full attention, and I found no peer-reviewed analysis of why. Negative results for linear hybrids at frontier scale are under-documented.

There are no independent, peer-reviewed apples-to-apples comparisons of Mamba-3, KDA and Gated DeltaNet-2 at more than 7B parameters and more than 1T tokens. Most head-to-heads are 1.3B-1.5B models on 100B tokens.
State-tracking gains are mostly shown on synthetic tasks (parity, group words). Their effect on real reasoning or code benchmarks in production hybrids is not established.
Inference-cost claims (KV cache savings, TPOT speedups) are vendor-measured with different serving stacks. Standardized benchmarks across vLLM/SGLang are missing.
I did not verify within budget: log-linear attention, PaTH attention, Hunyuan-TurboS, Samba/Hymba, Jet-Nemotron, MiniMax-M1, and Ring-linear/Ling hybrids. These may deserve inclusion.
Several venue labels (DeltaProduct, RWKV-7, Jamba) and the citation edges are from memory rather than verified against the papers' reference lists in this session.

papers.title: Image-based table recognition: data, model, and evaluation
papers.role: Foundational dataset + image-to-markup model (PubTabNet, EDD, TEDS)
papers.reason: Introduced PubTabNet: 568k table images paired with HTML. Also proposed the encoder-dual-decoder model, which decodes structure and cell OCR together, and the TEDS metric.
papers.quote: we develop the largest publicly available table recognition dataset PubTabNet (this https URL), containing 568k table images with corresponding structured HTML representation.

papers.title: PubTables-1M: Towards comprehensive table extraction from unstructured documents
papers.role: Foundational detection + structure dataset (and Table Transformer baseline)
papers.reason: About one million tables labelled for both detection and structure. It names oversegmentation as a ground-truth inconsistency in earlier datasets and fixes it with a canonicalization step.
papers.quote: It also addresses a significant source of ground truth inconsistency observed in prior datasets called oversegmentation, using a novel canonicalization procedure.

papers.title: TableFormer: Table Structure Understanding with Transformers
papers.reason: Swaps PubTabNet's OCR decoder for a cell bounding-box decoder, so cell text can be read from the PDF itself. This separates recognizing structure from recognizing text.
papers.quote: we introduce a new object detection decoder for table-cells. In this way, we can obtain the content of the table-cells from program-matic PDF's directly from the PDF source and avoid the training of the custom OCR decoders.

papers.title: TableBank: A Benchmark Dataset for Table Detection and Recognition
papers.reason: A large set of 417K tables for detection and recognition, labelled automatically (weak supervision) from Word and LaTeX source files.
papers.quote: We present TableBank, a new image-based table detection and recognition dataset built with novel weak supervision from Word and Latex documents on the internet.

papers.title: Aligning benchmark datasets for table structure recognition
papers.reason: Shows that annotations are inconsistent across datasets: when a Table Transformer (TATR) trained on FinTabNet is tested on ICDAR-2013, exact-match accuracy is only 42%, and it rises after the datasets are aligned.
papers.quote: even if a dataset's annotations are self-consistent, there may be significant inconsistency across datasets, which can harm the performance of models trained and evaluated on them.

papers.title: GriTS: Grid table similarity metric for table structure recognition
papers.reason: A metric that scores the predicted table as a matrix. One score covers cell topology, cell location and cell content.
papers.quote: Unlike prior metrics, GriTS evaluates the correctness of a predicted table directly in its natural form as a matrix.

papers.title: Optimized Table Tokenization for Table Structure Recognition
papers.reason: Replaces HTML output with a 5-token structure language. Sequences are about half as long and inference about twice as fast.
papers.quote: We propose a new, optimised table-structure language (OTSL) with a minimized vocabulary and specific rules.

papers.title: Complicated Table Structure Recognition
papers.reason: Treats structure recognition as predicting relations between cells with a graph neural network. Also releases SciTSR, which focuses on spanning cells.
papers.quote: it takes table cells as input, and then recognizes the table structures by predicting relations among cells.

papers.title: Global Table Extractor (GTE): A Framework for Joint Table Identification and Cell Structure Recognition Using Visual Context
papers.role: Joint detection + cell structure; source of FinTabNet

papers.quote: We present Global Table Extractor (GTE), a vision-guided systematic framework for joint table detection and cell structured recognition

papers.title: CascadeTabNet: An approach for end to end table detection and structure recognition from image-based documents
papers.reason: A single Cascade Mask R-CNN that finds tables and their body cells together. Evaluated on ICDAR 2013, ICDAR 2019 and TableBank.
papers.quote: We propose CascadeTabNet: a Cascade mask Region-based CNN High-Resolution Network (Cascade mask R-CNN HRNet) based model that detects the regions of tables and recognizes the structural body cells

papers.title: TSRFormer: Table Structure Recognition with Transformers
papers.reason: Predicts separator lines with a DETR-style detection transformer, framed as line regression, for distorted tables.
papers.quote: we formulate table separation line prediction as a line regression problem instead of an image segmentation problem and propose a new two-stage DETR based separator prediction approach

papers.title: TRUST: An Accurate and End-to-End Table structure Recognizer Using Splitting-based Transformers
papers.reason: Splits the problem into two jointly trained parts: splitting rows and columns, then merging grid cells. Each cell gets both physical coordinates and logical row/column indices.

papers.title: UniTable: Towards a Unified Framework for Table Recognition via Self-Supervised Pretraining

papers.reason: Argues that detection metrics and structure metrics such as TEDS do not measure the same thing.

papers.reason: Starts from OCR output and uses a transformer to predict word-pair relations (same row, column, header or table) for both detection and structure.
