answer.summary:
**Three separate tasks.** Table recognition splits into three parts:
- **Table detection (TD):** finding where tables are on the page. Main sources: TableBank, CascadeTabNet, GTE, RobusTabNet, and the detection subset of PubTables-1M.
- **Cell structure recognition (TSR):** recovering rows, columns, spanning cells and headers.
- **Text recognition (OCR / TCR):** reading the text inside each cell.

TabRecSet states the TD/TSR/TCR split directly. Some systems keep OCR separate: TableFormer reads cell text from the PDF, TableMaster uses separate text-line detection and recognition, and DELTA has its own OCR step. Others read text as part of one model: PubTabNet's EDD, UniTable, and VLM-based TRivia.

**Families of structure methods.**
- **Image-to-markup:** a transformer outputs HTML tokens. Examples are EDD, TableFormer, TableMaster and UniTable. OTSL is an alternative output language with 5 tokens instead of HTML's 28+, and it about halves sequence length.
- **Detection or splitting with transformers:** DETR-style models detect rows, columns or separator lines, then merge. Examples are the Table Transformer from PubTables-1M, TSRFormer, TRUST and SepFormer. These give exact cell geometry but depend on post-processing.
- **Graph and relation models:** GraphTSR, TGRNet and ClusterTabNet predict relations between cells or words, or each cell's logical position.
- **Vision-language models (2025–2026):** TRivia is the main example; DELTA instead uses a modular, text-based pipeline.

**Limitations of the data and evaluation, from the sources.**
- Labels are generated automatically from PubMed Central XML or Word/LaTeX files, so they lean toward scientific papers and can be inconsistent. PubTables-1M names oversegmentation as a problem in earlier datasets.
- Datasets disagree with each other. A TATR model trained on FinTabNet reaches only 42% exact match on ICDAR-2013, and aligning the datasets raises this substantially.
- Detection metrics do not line up with structure metrics like TEDS (2312.00699).
- Whole-document scores hide where failures happen (FormStruct-Bench).
- Models trained on PubTables-1M and FinTabNet make errors on business documents (RAPTOR).
- Scenes outside clean documents need new data: photographed tables (TabRecSet), construction documents (CISOL, not included in the list), and synthetic natural-scene tables (SNSTab in BGTR).
gaps: Semantic Scholar timed out and OpenAlex was rate-limited (HTTP 429) on 2026-10-08, so I couldn't expand the citation graph and have no citation counts for most papers. The citation links come only from explicit mentions in abstracts and are incomplete. Some likely links are not asserted: OTSL→TableFormer, GriTS→PubTables-1M, TableMaster→PubTabNet.

These well-known papers are not in arXiv or I couldn't verify them, so they are left out: DeepDeSRT (2017), the ICDAR 2013 and ICDAR 2019 cTDaR competition papers, SPLERGE (Tensmeyer et al. 2019), DeepTabStR, the TIES graph network, and the WTW / Cycle-CenterNet wild-table dataset. Several of these are the original works on detection and splitting.

Other recent papers I saw but did not list: BGTR/SNSTab (2609.08705), ConRTF (2607.00734), CISOL (2501.15469), TabSniper (2412.12827), MuTabNet (2404.13268), and EMBLEM/MANDALA, a multi-script detection dataset (2609.08330).

General document-parsing models and benchmarks that include tables, such as Nougat, Donut, OmniDocBench and the Docling technical report, are not covered, and I didn't check how VLM performance compares with specialist structure models.
All quotes are from abstracts. I didn't read the full texts, so the numbers on dataset limitations come only from the abstracts.

answer.summary:
I found 25 papers. Citation Lens could only search arXiv: Semantic Scholar timed out and OpenAlex was rate-limited, and both citation-graph expansions failed. So citation counts and graph edges are missing. The papers come from an arXiv search, two batches of abstract reads and one web search.

**Three tasks to keep apart:**
- **Table detection** finds where tables are on a page. Key work: TableBank, GTE-Table, CascadeTabNet, and Revisiting Table Detection Datasets with its merged Open-Tables set.
- **Table structure recognition** recovers rows, columns, spanning cells and headers. Key work: TATR, TableFormer, TSRFormer, TABLET, FastTab.
- **Cell-content recognition (OCR)** reads the text inside cells. TableFormer avoids it by taking text from the PDF. TabStructNet works without OCR at all. The EDD model, the multi-task model, the multi-cell decoder and UniTable learn it jointly with structure. ClusterTabNet assumes OCR output already exists.

**Main approaches:**
- **Transformer structure recognition:**
  - Image-to-markup decoders that output HTML or a token sequence: PubTabNet's EDD, TableFormer, VAST, UniTable, UniTabNet.
  - DETR-style detectors that find rows, columns and cells as objects: TATR and TSRFormer's separator regression.
  - Encoder-only split-merge models: TABLET, FastTab.
- **Alternative representations:**
  - OTSL, a 5-token structure language with about half the sequence length of HTML.
  - Graph or relation outputs that link cells or words: GraphTSR (SciTSR), ClusterTabNet.
  - Direct grid prediction: FastTab.
  - The 2025 shift is toward general vision-language models: TRivia's self-supervised fine-tuning, and NGTR's training-free tool use, which found low-quality images to be the main bottleneck.

**Datasets:** TableBank, PubTabNet, FinTabNet (from GTE), SciTSR and PubTables-1M dominate. Most are labeled automatically from scientific or financial PDFs.

**Dataset and evaluation limitations, from the sources:**
- PubTables-1M identifies oversegmentation as a source of inconsistent ground truth in earlier datasets.
- In Aligning benchmark datasets, the model stays fixed and only the labels are cleaned and aligned. Exact-match accuracy on ICDAR-2013 then rises from 65% to 75% (training on PubTables-1M) and from 42% to 65% (training on FinTabNet). So scores partly measure label quality.
- Revisiting Table Detection Datasets reports noisy, inconsistent detection data drawn from few sources.
- On metrics: GriTS argues for scoring tables as matrices rather than with TEDS, and Rethinking Detection Based TSR shows that detection metrics do not match TSR metrics. FormStruct-Bench (2026) says aggregate scores do not show where structure fails.
gaps: Semantic Scholar timed out and OpenAlex returned HTTP 429 or throttling, so both research_expand calls failed. There are no graph-verified citation counts or edges. Each listed citation is inferred from the citing paper's abstract (it names the cited dataset or model, e.g. TableFormer improving on PubTabNet's encoder-dual-decoder, or training and evaluating on PubTabNet, FinTabNet, PubTables-1M or SciTSR). The OTSL→TableFormer, OTSL→PubTabNet and UniTable→PubTabNet links come from my own background knowledge or a web snippet, not from a reference list I checked.

Some foundational or influential papers were not verified and are left out: DeepDeSRT (2017), the ICDAR 2013 and ICDAR 2019 cTDaR competitions, SPLERGE (split-merge), LGPMA (abstract was read and it is relevant, but it was cut for space), TGRNet, the WTW wired-table dataset, SEM/SEMv2, and the DETR and Mask R-CNN detector papers.
Known recent methods such as TFLOP and SPRINT were not found under their names in this search, so they are not included.

Domain and boundary datasets were left out of the list: CISOL (construction), TabSniper (bank statements), RAPTOR (product tables; a post-processing layer on TATR), TC-OCR, Table Detection in the Wild, MANDALA/EMBLEM (multi-script detection), CTE, and ConRTF (2026 real-time DETR-style structure recognition).

Coverage is thin for handwritten, historical, camera-captured, multilingual and non-scientific tables, and for general document-parsing VLMs (e.g. OCR-free document models and large multimodal LLMs) evaluated on table recognition.
Search date: 2026-10-08. Abstracts were truncated by the tool; quotes come only from the visible portions.

answer.summary:
I made all 8 allowed tool calls (four searches and four page fetches). Several fetches would only give short excerpts or paraphrases of abstracts, so most quotes come from my memory of the abstracts, not from text I checked in this session. The InstructTable quote and the OTSL and UniTable fragments come from fetched pages. The TABLET, TSRFormer, PubTables-v2 and PDF-parser-benchmark quotes come from search snippets. Quotes left empty are ones I wasn't sure enough of to reproduce word for word. Some papers were listed without checking their pages here: SPLERGE, CascadeTabNet, OmniDocBench, VAST, the GNN paper, Cycle-CenterNet/WTW, DeepDeSRT and the ICDAR competitions. I didn't open TRivia's content beyond a snippet that showed only references. Only the InstructTable citation links were checked in its text and the PubTables-v2 → PubTables-1M link is named in its abstract. Every other link comes from my knowledge of the papers and is unchecked.

**The three subtasks.** Table extraction splits into three jobs.
- **Table detection** finds table regions on a page. This was the focus of TableBank, DeepDeSRT, CascadeTabNet, ICDAR 2019 cTDaR Track A and PubTables-1M's detection split.
- **Structure recognition** recovers rows, columns, spanning cells and headers. Approaches include split-merge (SPLERGE, TSRFormer, TABLET), DETR-style object detection (TATR), image-to-markup (EDD, TableFormer, VAST) and graphs (GraphTSR, GNN models).
- **Cell content / OCR** reads the text in each cell. TableFormer and TATR often avoid OCR by taking the text from the PDF. EDD and UniTable predict the text themselves, and recent vision-language models (TRivia, the models in OmniDocBench and PubTables-v2) output structure and text together.

**Transformer approaches.**
- *Image-to-sequence* (TableFormer, VAST, UniTable) predicts HTML or OTSL tokens plus cell boxes. Simple, but autoregressive decoding is slow for large tables, which is why OTSL uses a shorter sequence.
- *Detection-based* (TATR) finds rows, columns and spanning cells as objects.
- *Separator-regression and encoder-only split-merge* (TSRFormer, TABLET) are faster and hold up better on dense or distorted tables.

**Alternative representations.** OTSL cuts the HTML vocabulary to about 5 tokens and always produces valid output. Graph formulations (GraphTSR, and POTATR's image-to-graph model in PubTables-v2) model cell relations directly and can handle tables that span pages.

**Dataset and evaluation limitations, with source evidence.**
- *Label noise drives scores.* "Aligning benchmark datasets" kept the TATR model fixed and only fixed labels. ICDAR-2013 exact match rose from 42% to 65% when trained on FinTabNet, and from 65% to 75% on PubTables-1M.
- *Oversegmentation.* PubTables-1M added canonicalization to fix this inconsistency in earlier datasets.
- *Narrow domains.* Most data are PubMed tables (PubTabNet, PubTables-1M), with FinTabNet covering financial reports.
- *Small, simple tables.* InstructTable notes that existing public datasets "predominantly feature small-scale tables with limited cell counts."
- *Cropped single tables.* PubTables-v2 argues that page-level and multi-page extraction have lacked annotated data.
- *Metrics mix error types.* TEDS combines structure and OCR errors. GriTS separates topology, content and location. A 2026 human study found TEDS (r=0.68) and GriTS (r=0.70) track human judgment much worse than an LLM judge (r=0.93).
- *Weak labels and limited coverage.* TableBank's structure labels have no cell coordinates. Photographed or distorted tables are covered mainly by WTW.
gaps: No standard benchmark scores detection, structure and OCR separately on the same full pages. Most TSR results use cropped tables with text from the PDF, which hides OCR errors.

Labels are inconsistent across datasets (PubTabNet, FinTabNet, PubTables-1M, SciTSR, ICDAR-2013), which hurts cross-dataset comparison. Fixing the labels shows large score changes, but no single agreed-upon cleaned benchmark exists.

Domains and languages are narrow: mostly English scientific and financial PDFs. There is little coverage of multilingual or right-to-left scripts, handwritten, historical or photographed tables beyond cTDaR-archival and WTW.
Large, dense and multi-page tables are underrepresented. PubTables-v2 and InstructTable's BCDSTab are early attempts, and the PubTables-v2 code and models had not been released when I checked.
Metric validity: TEDS and GriTS correlate only moderately with human judgments and can penalize harmless rendering differences. Semantic or LLM-judge metrics are new and not yet standardized.

End-to-end vision-language models are mostly evaluated on page-level parsing benchmarks (e.g., OmniDocBench). Few studies compare them directly with specialized TSR models under the same structure-only and OCR-only metrics.

Citation edges here were checked only for InstructTable (by fetching its text) and partly from the PubTables-v2 abstract. The rest come from my knowledge of the papers. I also couldn't confirm which of two 2025 papers named 'TABLET' InstructTable cites.

answer.summary:
**Three separate subtasks.** Most papers address only one or two of these, and scores are not comparable across them.
- **Table detection:** finding where tables are on the page. TableBank, the GTE paper, PubTables-1M/TATR (a DETR-based detector), RobusTabNet and DocLayNet-style layout models do this.
- **Cell structure recognition (TSR):** recovering rows, columns, spanning cells and headers from a cropped table.
- **Text recognition:** reading what is in each cell. Many TSR systems (TATR, TableFormer, TABLET) take this from the PDF text layer or an external OCR engine. End-to-end systems (EDD/PubTabNet, UniTable, TDATR, VLM parsers) generate it themselves.

**Model families for structure recognition.**
- **Image-to-markup transformers:** EDD, TableFormer, VAST and UniTable decode HTML tokens.
- **Alternative token representation:** OTSL (adopted by SPRINT and TABLET) replaces HTML with a compact grid language. That shortens sequences and guarantees a valid table.
- **Object-detection style:** TATR treats rows, columns and spanning cells as DETR objects.
- **Split-merge:** TSRFormer, RobusTabNet and TABLET first find row and column separators, then merge cells. TABLET's encoder-only labeling avoids autoregressive decoding, which makes it fast on dense tables.
- **Other alternatives:** graph or cell-based methods (SciTSR, LGPMA) and one-stage CenterNet-style models (Cycle-CenterNet, TableCenterNet).

**Evidence on dataset and evaluation limitations.**
- Benchmarks are mostly built by automatically matching PDFs to XML or HTML, which introduces label noise.
- PubTables-1M had to fix oversegmentation by canonicalizing labels.
- The "Aligning benchmark datasets" paper keeps the model fixed and shows that cleaning and aligning labels alone raises ICDAR-2013 exact match from 42% to 65% when trained on FinTabNet.
- TABLET found that FinTabNet's test labels were "incorrect or inconsistent", so some reported model errors were actually label errors.
- TEDS folds OCR errors into the structure score. GriTS scores topology, content and location separately, so the two kinds of error can be told apart.
- Most benchmarks use cropped, clean PDF renders. WTW and TabRecSet target camera-captured tables, PubTables-v2 targets full pages and multi-page tables, and OmniDocBench criticizes "simplified, unrealistic evaluation".
- Domain benchmarks such as ChemTable show that multimodal LLMs still lag on specialized tables. PubTables-v2 finds that small specialized models can match or beat VLMs on cropped-table extraction.
gaps: The 8-call budget meant only TABLET, Aligning, PubTables-v2 and OmniDocBench pages were opened directly. Several abstract quotes (PubTabNet, PubTables-1M, TableBank, DETR, WTW, GriTS, UniTable, TableFormer) are recalled from memory rather than re-checked; the OTSL quote is a fragment taken from a search-result summary. Unverified quotes were left empty where confidence was low.

Citation edges from TABLET were checked against its reference list. The other edges (PubTables-1M→DETR/PubTabNet, Aligning→PubTables-1M/FinTabNet, PubTables-v2→PubTables-1M, OTSL→TableFormer, SPRINT→OTSL, TableFormer→PubTabNet) rest on the method or evaluation descriptions, not on checked reference lists.
TDATR (2026), CISOL (2025) and InstructTable (2026) were only seen in search results; their methods and claims were not verified.
No benchmark found clearly scores detection, structure and OCR jointly but separately across full pages. PubTables-v2's content-scoring protocol was not confirmed.

Coverage is weak for non-English and handwritten tables, borderless or rotated tables beyond WTW, and large VLM document parsers (e.g., MinerU2.5, PaddleOCR/SLANet, Docling), which mainly report results on PubTabNet/TEDS.
Test-set label noise (FinTabNet, PubTabNet) means small SOTA differences on these benchmarks may not be meaningful; there is no widely adopted cleaned test split.

papers.reason: The standard one-shot weight-only PTQ method. It quantizes column by column and uses approximate inverse-Hessian error compensation; most later work builds on it.
papers.quote: we address this challenge, and propose GPTQ, a new one-shot weight quantization method based on approximate second-order information, that is both highly-accurate and highly-efficient.

papers.reason: Uses activation statistics to find salient weight channels and scales them up, which avoids mixed precision. It is the main gradient-free alternative to GPTQ.

papers.role: Foundational: weight-and-activation (W8A8) quantization with outlier smoothing
papers.reason: Moves activation-outlier difficulty into the weights through an equivalent per-channel scaling. This is the key reference for the weight-and-activation regime.

papers.role: Foundational: discovery of emergent activation outliers and handling them with mixed precision
papers.reason: Showed that systematic outlier features dominate at scale and handled them by decomposing them into higher precision. This motivates nearly all later outlier work.

answer.summary:
I found 25 papers on post-training low-bit quantization of LLMs, from the 2022 foundations to work from late 2025. The citation graph could not be retrieved because the scholarly indexes were rate-limiting, so the eight citation links listed are only those named in the citing paper's abstract.

**Weight-only methods.** These target memory-bandwidth-bound decoding (SqueezeLLM argues this case).
- **Second-order reconstruction.** OBC/OBQ, then GPTQ: column-by-column rounding with inverse-Hessian error compensation. Recent theory recasts GPTQ as Babai's nearest-plane algorithm on a lattice. Its error bound only holds when no weights are clipped. The linearity-theorem paper argues that per-layer L2 objectives lack theoretical justification.
- **Activation-aware scaling.** AWQ protects about 1% of salient channels, chosen from activation statistics, through equivalent scaling instead of mixed precision. OmniQuant makes the clipping and scaling learnable, because hand-crafted parameters fail at extremely low bits.
- **Weight-outlier handling.** SpQR and SqueezeLLM store outlier weights sparsely in higher precision. QuIP, QuIP#, HIGGS and OptRot instead remove outliers with incoherence processing or rotations.
- **Codebook competitor.** AQLM (additive multi-codebook quantization), QuIP# (E8 lattice), GPTVQ (Hessian-guided vector quantization) and QTIP (trellis-coded quantization) beat scalar grids at 2–3 bits. The costs:
  - vector-quantization codebooks grow exponentially with dimension (QTIP);
  - GPTVQ needs hours of compute for a 70B model;
  - the best results depend on fine-tuning the compressed weights, which PV-Tuning says reaches diminishing returns for purely post-training methods.

**Weight-and-activation methods.** These are needed for INT8/INT4 compute speedups. The difficulty is activation outliers, first described in LLM.int8().
- SmoothQuant moves that difficulty from activations into the weights (W8A8). DuQuant shows smoothing fails on 'massive' outliers.
- QuaRot (random Hadamard rotations) and SpinQuant (learned rotations) reach W4A4 plus KV cache. SpinQuant finds that rotation choice alone can swing zero-shot reasoning accuracy by up to 13 points.
- OptRot finds rotations that help weight-only quantization perform worse at W4A4, so the two regimes trade off against each other.
- The FP4 study shows that small NVFP4 groups neutralize classic outlier mitigation.

**Limitations reported in the sources.**
- Accuracy drops for 1–10B models at 3–4 bits (SpQR).
- Calibration cost and fine-tuning dependence of codebook methods (GPTVQ, PV-Tuning).
- Errors build up over long chains of thought in reasoning models (ParoQuant).
- Hardware-format mismatch with MXFP4/NVFP4 (FP4 study).
- Evaluation studies (Li et al. 2024, ZeroQuant-V2, LLaMA3) report regime-dependent degradation.
gaps: The citation graph could not be expanded: Semantic Scholar and OpenAlex were rate-limiting or timing out for both expansion calls (search date 2026-10-08). The citation links come only from cited methods named in the citing paper's abstract (e.g., QuIP names OPTQ, i.e. GPTQ). Many real links (e.g., AWQ→GPTQ, QuaRot→SmoothQuant, AQLM→GPTQ/QuIP) are almost certainly present but unverified, so I omitted them.
Several abstracts were cut off at 1000 characters, so the quotes come from the visible part only. Headline numbers (perplexity, speedups) were not checked against the full papers.

The 2024-10 to 2026-10 window is thin on verified, highly cited work. I did not screen recent arXiv-only candidates seen in the search (AAAC activation-aware adaptive codebooks, QAM-W, ADMM-Q, Astro, OSAQ, ThinQuant, G²PTQ, JARQ, Scale Sensitivity in Low-Bit PTQ, Activation Sensitivity as a Unifying Principle), and their quality is unknown.

Not covered: KV-cache-only quantization, quantization-aware training (e.g., BitNet, EfficientQAT), mixed-precision allocation methods, and kernel/serving systems (e.g., Marlin, QServe). Also missing are other well-known PTQ papers not retrieved here: OSTQuant, FlatQuant, AffineQuant, QuantEase, BiLLM/PB-LLM (sub-2-bit), Atom and QuIK.
ZeroQuant-V2 has both an arXiv (2303.08302) and an AAAI DOI version. I listed only the arXiv version.

answer.summary:
Low-bit LLM post-training quantization has two families. Weight-only methods (W4/3/2 with A16) target memory-bandwidth-bound decoding. Weight-and-activation methods (W8A8, W4A8, W4A4) aim to speed up compute-bound large-batch serving.

Weight-only methods:
- **Second-order reconstruction:** OBC/OBQ led to GPTQ, which uses a Hessian-based update to quantize 175B models to 3–4 bits in hours. Follow-ups include GPTAQ, which addresses error accumulation from GPTQ's independent per-layer calibration, and QuIP's incoherence processing.
- **Activation-aware scaling:** AWQ scales salient channels using calibration activations instead of solving a reconstruction. SINQ (2025) approximates the same column scales without calibration data.
- **Outlier handling:** SpQR and SqueezeLLM keep a small sparse set of outlier weights at high precision and quantize the rest.
- **Codebooks / vector quantization:** AQLM's additive multi-codebooks and QuIP#'s E8 lattice beat scalar grids below 3 bits. QTIP's trellis codes get around the exponential codebook-size limit. PV-Tuning shows these methods increasingly depend on fine-tuning.

Weight-and-activation methods face activation outliers, documented in LLM.int8(). SmoothQuant moves that difficulty into the weights for W8A8. OmniQuant learns clipping and equivalent transforms. QuaRot and SpinQuant use (learned) rotations to reach W4A4KV4. PrefixQuant handles token-wise outliers. QServe co-designs W4A8KV4 kernels.

Limitations supported by the sources:
- 3–4-bit quantization hurts small 1–10B models (SpQR).
- Pure PTQ reaches diminishing returns at 1–2 bits (PV-Tuning).
- VQ codebooks grow exponentially with dimension (QTIP).
- Layer-wise error metrics lack theoretical justification (HIGGS).
- GPTQ calibrates each layer independently (GPTAQ).
- Random rotations vary by up to 13 points (SpinQuant).
- Channel-wise methods miss token-wise outliers (PrefixQuant).
- INT4 dequantization adds 20–90% runtime overhead in serving (QServe).
- Outliers still degrade weight-only PTQ as of 2026 (Astro).

The large evaluation in 'Give Me BF16' finds W4A16 competitive with 8-bit and the most cost-efficient for synchronous deployment, while W8A8 dominates asynchronous (high-throughput) serving.

answer.summary:
I used 8 research calls. These quotes were checked against sources during this session: AQLM, QTIP, DuQuant, FlatQuant, OstQuant, GPTAQ, HIGGS, the BF16 study and the undertrained-LLM study. The other quotes are abstract wording I recalled without checking (GPTQ, AWQ, SmoothQuant, QuIP, QuaRot), and they should be spot-checked. Where I had no quote I could rely on, I left the field empty. I listed only citations I had good reason to believe exist, such as baselines or direct derivations. A few were confirmed by this session's sources (GPTAQ→GPTQ/OBC, FlatQuant→QuaRot/SpinQuant, BF16 study→GPTQ/AWQ). The rest come from my knowledge of each paper's baselines and were not opened to check.

How the approaches compare:
(1) Second-order reconstruction (OBC→GPTQ→GPTAQ, and the Babai-lattice theory) minimizes Hessian-weighted layer output error. It is fast and is the default for W4A16/W3A16. GPTQ's error bound holds only when no weights are clipped. Its error also builds up from layer to layer, which GPTAQ addresses with asymmetric calibration.
(2) Activation-aware scaling (AWQ, and OmniQuant's learned version) uses activation magnitudes to protect salient weight channels with equivalent scaling. It is robust and needs no reconstruction, but it is mainly a weight-only technique.
(3) Outlier handling takes two forms. Weight-only methods isolate outliers sparsely (SpQR, SqueezeLLM). Weight-and-activation methods start from LLM.int8() mixed precision and SmoothQuant's migration of outliers from activations to weights (W8A8). They then move to rotations for W4A4 (QuaRot Hadamard → SpinQuant learned → DuQuant rotation+permutation for massive outliers → FlatQuant/OstQuant learned affine or orthogonal-plus-scaling transforms). These methods are needed because activation outliers make W4A4 far harder than W4A16.
(4) Competing codebook/vector quantization (QuIP#'s E8 lattice, AQLM's additive multi-codebooks, QTIP's trellis codes, with PV-Tuning fine-tuning on top) dominates at 2–3 bits weight-only. It costs more calibration or fine-tuning compute and needs specialized decode kernels.

Weight-only vs weight-and-activation: in the large evaluations, W4A16 (GPTQ/AWQ) and W8A8 are near-lossless and W4A16 is the most efficient for latency-bound serving. W4A4 still loses accuracy even with rotations. In the BF16 study, W8A8-INT lost about 1–3% per task on average and FP8 was near-lossless.

Limitations reported in the sources: reasoning models and harder tasks degrade more below W4A16/W8A8. Heavily trained (data-saturated) and smaller models degrade more under low-bit PTQ, as with LLaMA3 and the 100T-token scaling laws. Sub-3-bit PTQ needs extra fine-tuning (PV-Tuning). One evaluation (2507.17417) reports that rotation gains mostly disappear for MXFP4/NVFP4 formats. Data-free weight rotations (OptRot) can help weight quantization while hurting W4A4.
gaps: Citation edges were not checked against reference lists. They come from the baselines and derivations named in the papers, plus a few confirmed by this session's search results; a citation-graph tool would add more and confirm them.

I could not confirm the abstract wording for OBC, SpQR, SqueezeLLM, OmniQuant, QuIP#, SpinQuant, PV-Tuning, the Babai paper, the reasoning study or the LLaMA3 study, so their quote fields are empty or very short.
Recent hardware-format work is under-covered: MXFP4/NVFP4 microscaling PTQ and FP4 weight-activation methods from 2025–2026 are only mentioned through the 2507.17417 evaluation.

Not covered: KV-cache quantization, mixed-precision bit allocation beyond HIGGS, MoE-specific PTQ, and recent layer-wise rotation methods (e.g., ReSpinQuant 2604.11080, OptRot 2512.24124), which were found but not checked in depth.
Few independent head-to-head studies compare codebook methods (AQLM/QuIP#/QTIP) and scalar methods under equal end-to-end latency and calibration compute.

Beyond perplexity and zero-shot accuracy, evidence is still thin on long-context, multilingual and safety degradation from low-bit PTQ (e.g., 2511.07842 on safety-preserving PTQ was seen but not checked).

papers.reason: Shows that pure PTQ codebook methods such as AQLM gain substantially from fine-tuning at 1–2 bits, which suggests PTQ alone has a ceiling at very low bit-widths.

answer.summary:
There are four main strands.

1. **Second-order reconstruction (weight-only).** OBC/OBQ led to GPTQ, which uses an approximate Hessian to compensate rounding error one layer at a time. It became the default 3–4-bit W4A16 method. GPTAQ (2025) fixes GPTQ's independent per-layer calibration by matching full-precision outputs. HIGGS (2025) provides a linearity theorem that justifies layer-wise objectives and shows that a data-free approach (Hadamard rotations plus MSE-optimal grids) can compete.

2. **Activation-aware scaling.** AWQ scales the salient weight channels using activation statistics and needs no reconstruction (weight-only). SmoothQuant uses the same equivalent-scaling idea to move activation outliers into the weights for W8A8. OmniQuant makes both the clipping and the scaling learnable.

3. **Outlier handling.** Outliers can be kept apart in higher precision (LLM.int8() for activations; SpQR and SqueezeLLM keep weights sparse). Or the distribution can be reshaped:
   - QuIP introduced incoherence processing.
   - QuaRot and SpinQuant use fixed or learned rotations for W4A4KV4.
   - DuQuant, FlatQuant and OstQuant (2024–25) add permutations, learnable affine transforms, or combined orthogonal and scaling transforms. FlatQuant reports less than 1% accuracy loss at W4A4 on LLaMA-3-70B.

4. **Codebook approaches.** These compete with scalar grids in the 2–3-bit weight-only regime. AQLM uses additive multi-codebooks, QuIP# uses E8 lattices with Hadamard rotations, GPTVQ applies Hessian-guided VQ, and QTIP uses trellis coding to avoid exponential codebooks. PV-Tuning shows that fine-tuning still helps beyond PTQ.

**Weight-only vs. weight-and-activation.** Weight-only methods (GPTQ, AWQ, SpQR, QuIP#, AQLM, QTIP, HIGGS) reduce memory and speed up memory-bound decoding. They are near-lossless at 4 bits, and codebooks are needed to stay usable at 2 bits. Weight-and-activation methods (SmoothQuant, QuaRot, SpinQuant, FlatQuant, OstQuant, QServe) must also deal with activation and KV outliers so that low-precision GEMMs can be used. They are lossless at W8A8, but at W4A4 they still lose accuracy, and QServe reports kernel and dequantization overhead.

**Limitations from the sources.**
- "Give Me BF16" finds FP8 lossless, INT8 losing about 1–3%, and W4A16 most cost-efficient for synchronous serving, with W8A8 better for batched serving.
- Ouyang et al. find that low-bit degradation grows with the number of training tokens, which may make heavily trained future models harder to quantize.
- Liu et al. find that quantization below W4A16 or W8A8 hurts reasoning models, more so on harder tasks and for RL-trained models.
gaps: The research budget allowed no full-text page opens. Quotes for older papers come from memory of their abstracts, and quotes were left empty where unsure. The citation links reflect how the papers build on and compare with each other and were not checked against reference lists.

Papers not covered for lack of budget: KV-cache-only quantization (e.g., KIVI, KVQuant), FP4/MXFP4/NVFP4 microscaling formats, and 2025–26 work on quantizing MoE and very large models (e.g., DeepSeek-V3 or R1).
There are few standardized comparisons of codebook methods against rotated scalar methods at equal kernel speed and on equal hardware.
Most results are on perplexity and zero-shot benchmarks for LLaMA-family models. Evidence on long-context, multilingual, safety and agentic tasks is limited.
The scaling-law limitation (Ouyang et al.) was studied only on Pythia models up to 12B and 300B tokens, and only with GPTQ. It is unclear whether it holds for multi-stage-trained frontier models.
Calibration-data sensitivity and overfitting of learnable-transform methods (OmniQuant, FlatQuant, OstQuant, SpinQuant) are not systematically quantified in the sources gathered.
Papers from 2026 onward were not searched specifically and may be underrepresented.

weight_quantization-web-r2.title: SpinQuant: LLM quantization with learned rotations
weight_quantization-web-r2.reason: Optimizes the rotation matrices instead of using random ones, which narrows the W4A4 accuracy gap.

paper.title: SpinQuant: LLM quantization with learned rotations

label.reason: Learned rotations mitigate outliers in W4A4 and cache quantization; documents sensitivity to random rotations.

weight_quantization-web-r2.title: OmniQuant: Omnidirectionally Calibrated Quantization for Large Language Models
weight_quantization-web-r2.role: Learnable clipping and equivalent transforms; covers both weight-only and weight-and-activation
weight_quantization-web-r2.reason: Generalizes SmoothQuant and AWQ scaling into learnable block-wise transformations.
weight_quantization-web-r2.quote: OmniQuant comprises two innovative components including Learnable Weight Clipping (LWC) and Learnable Equivalent Transformation (LET)

paper.title: OmniQuant: Omnidirectionally Calibrated Quantization for Large Language Models

label.reason: Learns equivalent transformations and weight clipping for low-bit PTQ across weight-only and weight-and-activation settings.

weight_quantization-web-r2.title: FlatQuant: Flatness Matters for LLM Quantization
weight_quantization-web-r2.reason: Shows that rotated or scaled distributions can stay steep. Per-layer Kronecker affine transforms make them flatter.
weight_quantization-web-r2.quote: less than 1% accuracy drop for W4A4 quantization on the LLaMA-3-70B model, surpassing SpinQuant by 7.5%

paper.title: FlatQuant: Flatness Matters for LLM Quantization

label.reason: Learned affine transformations flatten outliers for W4A4 quantization, supporting comparison with weight-only approaches.

weight_quantization-web-r2.title: OstQuant: Refining Large Language Model Quantization with Orthogonal and Scaling Transformations for Better Distribution Fitting
weight_quantization-web-r2.role: Recent (ICLR 2025): combines orthogonal and scaling transforms
weight_quantization-web-r2.reason: Learns rotation and scaling together and reports both W4-only and W4A4KV4 results.

paper.title: OstQuant: Refining Large Language Model Quantization with Orthogonal and Scaling Transformations for Better Distribution Fitting

label.reason: Learned orthogonal and scaling transformations address heavy-tailed weights and activations in LLM post-training quantization.

weight_quantization-web-r2.title: Pushing the Limits of Large Language Model Quantization via the Linearity Theorem
weight_quantization-web-r2.role: Recent (NAACL 2025): theory for layer-wise error plus data-free HIGGS
weight_quantization-web-r2.reason: Links layer-wise error to perplexity. Data-free Hadamard rotations with MSE-optimal grids beat NF4.
weight_quantization-web-r2.quote: combines Hadamard rotations and MSE-optimal grids, dubbed HIGGS, which outperforms all prior data-free approaches

paper.title: Pushing the Limits of Large Language Model Quantization via the Linearity Theorem

label.reason: HIGGS combines Hadamard rotations with optimized quantization grids and theoretically connects reconstruction error to perplexity.

weight_quantization-web-r2.title: GPTAQ: Efficient Finetuning-Free Quantization for Asymmetric Calibration
weight_quantization-web-r2.reason: Extends GPTQ in closed form to correct errors that accumulate across layers.
weight_quantization-web-r2.quote: Unlike the previous GPTQ method, which independently calibrates each layer, we always match the quantized layer's output to the exact output in the full-precision model

paper.title: GPTAQ: Efficient Finetuning-Free Quantization for Asymmetric Calibration

label.reason: Extends GPTQ using OBS-derived asymmetric reconstruction to compensate accumulated layer quantization errors.

weight_quantization-web-r2.title: SqueezeLLM: Dense-and-Sparse Quantization
weight_quantization-web-r2.reason: Sensitivity-weighted k-means non-uniform quantization, with outliers kept in sparse form.

paper.title: SqueezeLLM: Dense-and-Sparse Quantization

label.reason: Combines sensitivity-weighted nonuniform weight quantization with sparse high-precision retention of outliers and sensitive weights.

weight_quantization-web-r2.title: GPTVQ: The Blessing of Dimensionality for LLM Quantization
weight_quantization-web-r2.reason: Applies Hessian-guided updates to vector quantization and shows that higher dimensionality improves the size-accuracy trade-off.

paper.title: GPTVQ: The Blessing of Dimensionality for LLM Quantization

label.reason: Post-training vector weight codebooks combine Hessian reconstruction updates with measured LLM compression and decompression tradeoffs.

weight_quantization-web-r2.title: QServe: W4A8KV4 Quantization and System Co-design for Efficient LLM Serving
weight_quantization-web-r2.reason: Documents the runtime dequantization overhead of W4A4 and INT4 on GPUs and proposes W4A8KV4 instead.

paper.title: QServe: W4A8KV4 Quantization and System Co-design for Efficient LLM Serving

label.reason: W4A8KV4 serving study documents dequantization overhead and deployment limitations of existing weight-only INT4 methods.

weight_quantization-web-r2.title: DuQuant: Distributing Outliers via Dual Transformation Makes Stronger Quantized LLMs
weight_quantization-web-r2.role: Outlier handling: rotation plus permutation, W4A4
weight_quantization-web-r2.reason: Targets massive and normal activation outliers with block rotations and zigzag permutation.

paper.title: DuQuant: Distributing Outliers via Dual Transformation Makes Stronger Quantized LLMs

label.reason: Rotation and permutation explicitly address massive activation outliers, informing weight-and-activation quantization comparisons.

weight_quantization-web-r2.title: "Give Me BF16 or Give Me Death"? Accuracy-Performance Trade-Offs in LLM Quantization
weight_quantization-web-r2.role: Recent large-scale evaluation (ACL 2025); limitations and deployment guidance
weight_quantization-web-r2.reason: More than 500,000 evaluations comparing FP8, INT8 W8A8 and INT4 W4A16. The best format depends on the deployment regime.
weight_quantization-web-r2.quote: FP8 weight and activation quantization (W8A8-FP) is lossless across all model scales

paper.title: "Give Me BF16 or Give Me Death"? Accuracy-Performance Trade-Offs in LLM Quantization

label.reason: Directly compares W4A16 and W8A8 accuracy and serving performance, supporting deployment-specific limitations.

weight_quantization-web-r2.title: Low-Bit Quantization Favors Undertrained LLMs: Scaling Laws for Quantized LLMs with 100T Training Tokens
weight_quantization-web-r2.reason: Smaller models trained on more tokens degrade more under GPTQ low-bit quantization.
weight_quantization-web-r2.quote: low-bit quantization performance of future models, which are expected to be trained with over 100 trillion tokens, may NOT be desirable

paper.title: Low-Bit Quantization Favors Undertrained LLMs: Scaling Laws for Quantized LLMs with 100T Training Tokens

label.reason: Provides empirical low-bit quantization limitations linked to model size and training-token count.

weight_quantization-web-r2.title: Quantization Hurts Reasoning? An Empirical Study on Quantized Reasoning Models
weight_quantization-web-r2.reason: W8A8 and W4A16 are close to lossless. Lower bit-widths and harder tasks degrade reasoning models substantially.
weight_quantization-web-r2.quote: evaluating the open-sourced DeepSeek-R1-Distilled Qwen and LLaMA families ranging from 1.5B to 70B parameters, and QwQ-32B

paper.title: Quantization Hurts Reasoning? An Empirical Study on Quantized Reasoning Models

label.reason: Documents reasoning accuracy limitations across weight-only, activation, and cache quantization at different bitwidths.

weight_quantization-web-r2.title: PV-Tuning: Beyond Straight-Through Estimation for Extreme LLM Compression
